notes: Only the English pages carry front matter links and AI briefs (ai: see src/ai/BRIEFS.md); a French or Portuguese page with the same slug inherits them, and translationOf names the English page. A brief is used by the AI only when its status is reviewed.

pages.title: Leveraging AI for Analysis and Interpretation

sections.heading: Leveraging AI for Analysis and Interpretation
sections.text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) can be a powerful tool to enhance the efficiency, depth, and accessibility of data analysis and interpretation. It can support analysts in rapidly exploring datasets, identifying patterns, summarizing trends, and generating initial visualizations and insights. AI can also help structure written explanations, translate technical findings for different audiences, and synthesize relevant evidence from large volumes of information. When used well, AI can enable analysts to spend less time on routine or time-intensive tasks and more time on critical thinking, such as contextualizing findings, building shared understanding, and tailoring messages to decision-makers' needs.

However, AI must be used thoughtfully, with sound professional judgment and clear accountability. It should not replace the analyst's role in interpreting results, assessing data limitations, or making context-specific judgments. AI-generated outputs may contain inaccuracies, overlook important nuances, or reflect biases in the underlying data. Therefore, outputs must always be reviewed, validated, and adapted.

Collaboration between data producers, analysts, and data users to interpret findings is also essential to build shared understanding and ownership. Final interpretations, conclusions, and recommendations should always remain grounded in human expertise, subject-matter expertise, and an understanding of the local context. Therefore, AI should be considered a support tool that amplifies and strengthens analysis and interpretation, but is not a substitute for critical thinking, judgment, and shared decision-making.

AI can amplify | AI must not replace
Analysis – Understanding what the data shows | 
Sharpening the definition of the problem or question

that the analysis should respond to | Framing the problem or question

that the analysis should respond to
Surfacing data quality issues

(e.g., incompleteness, inconsistencies, outliers, etc.) | Assessing data quality and fitness for use

, including reliability, comparability, limitations
Faster, deeper pattern detection;

connecting signals from across sources | Deciding

what patterns to look for

in the data and why
Structured comparisons

across time, geographies, subgroups, etc. | Determining

which comparisons are valid and relevant
Generating

clear visual summaries | Selecting appropriate visualizations

and defining what should be shown and compared
Interpretation – Understanding what the data means | 
Generating possible explanations

and hypotheses for trends and patterns, testing assumptions | Using context,

collective knowledge and experience

to identify likely explanations; whether relationships are causal and actionable
Presenting sets of options and scenarios for prioritization | Weighing up options

, deciding priorities;

owning decisions

and justifying choices
Surfacing counterarguments

and bias checks | Integrating stakeholder perspectives

, navigating power dynamics
Refining key messages

and adapting language, tone, and formats for different audiences | Judging what messages are most appropriate

and useful for each audience,

ensuring accuracy

sections.heading: What makes an effective prompt
sections.text:
- Be clear on the purpose – e.g., identify trends, show anomalies, interpret trends.
- Define the audience – e.g., analyst deep dive versus policymaker summary.
- Specify geography, time, and scope – e.g., country, administrative level, indicators, time period.
- Provide interpretation guidance – e.g., highlight gender and equity gaps, suggest possible explanations.
- Specify the output format – e.g., a slide deck, short narrative, comparison table.
- Set guardrails – e.g., stick to the data shown; flag uncertainty or data quality issues; avoid speculation beyond evidence; note assumptions and inferences.

Example of an effective prompt:

Using only the data provided, summarize key trends, identify patterns and outliers at national level, and highlight gender and equity differences. Clearly distinguish between what the data shows (analysis) and what it may mean (interpretation). Explicitly identify data limitations, assumptions, and sources of uncertainty.

sections.heading: Using AI prompts to support gender analysis and interpretation
sections.text:
Below is an example of a prompt that you can adapt and paste into the DataSuite Assistant to generate an initial gender analysis and interpretation. Please incorporate your country's data into the prompt.

The AI output is designed to provide a starting point only. It will highlight key assumptions and suggest reflection questions that your team can use to guide your discussions. All AI outputs should be carefully reviewed and refined based on your team's knowledge, expertise, and country context, focusing on the findings that are most relevant for your intended audience.

These prompts can be used to generate findings for your CAM analytical report or used to create a short summary for the chartbook.

Please reach out to Lior Idit Miller (lmiller9@worldbank.org) and/or Elizabeth Hazel (ehazel1@jhu.edu) for questions or support at the CAM or afterwards. More details are available on the MAGE project website.

sections.heading: Prompt for country analytical teams
sections.text:
Using only the data points below, generate a gender-lens interpretation of maternal health in this country. The AI should provide an initial interpretation that requires country team review, validation, and refinement.

The interpretation should be brief and concise. For each section, the AI should flag assumptions and pose reflective questions for teams to consider based on their contextual knowledge.

Country data:

- Country name: [Add country name here]
- Demand for family planning satisfied by modern contraceptives: [Add country data here]
- Unmet need for family planning: [Add country data here]
- ANC 4+ visits coverage: [Add country data here]
- ANC first trimester coverage: [Add country data here]
- Institutional delivery coverage: [Add country data here]
- Postnatal care coverage: [Add country data here]
- C-section rate: [Add country data here]
- Urban/rural institutional delivery gap (percentage points): [Add country data here]
- Maternal education institutional delivery gap (percentage points): [Add country data here]

Output format:

Create a bold heading for this section called "Draft interpretation for country team review". Include this opening text: Access to essential maternal health services reflects broader gender inequities that shape women's autonomy over their reproductive health and their ability to seek care.

Organize the findings by subheading: Family planning; Antenatal care; Delivery and postnatal care; Equity. Then for each subheading include "Interpretation", "Assumptions for team validation", and "Reflection questions". Reflection questions should be limited to the specific assumptions mentioned and no more than 3.

Generate policy message options:

Based on the data provided, generate 4-5 bullet point illustrative policy messages that country teams can use as starting points for discussion. These should be:

- Directly linked to specific data points provided
- Policy-relevant and potentially actionable
- Framed through a gender and equity lens
- Concise (1-2 sentences each)

Each bullet should identify the data-driven finding and its gender/equity implication. Present these as suggestions rather than recommendations.

Include this closing text: These are illustrative examples intended to spark discussion. Country teams should validate for accuracy and relevance to current policy priorities, adapt language to local context, or develop alternative messages that better reflect their strategic objectives. Teams may select, combine, revise, or replace these options entirely.

sections.heading: Example of an AI output using Malawi 2025 CAM data
sections.text: For illustrative purposes only.

sections.heading: Draft interpretation for country team review
sections.text: Access to essential maternal health services reflects broader gender inequities that shape women's autonomy over their reproductive health and their ability to seek care.

sections.heading: Family planning
sections.text:
Interpretation: Malawi demonstrates relatively strong performance in modern contraceptive uptake (80.6% demand satisfied), suggesting progress in women's access to fertility control. However, the persistent 20% unmet need indicates that one in five women who wish to delay or prevent pregnancy cannot do so. This gap may reflect gendered barriers including limited decision-making power, partner opposition, or restricted access for certain groups such as adolescents and unmarried women.

Assumptions for team validation:

- The unmet need figure captures women across all age groups and marital statuses equally
- High contraceptive satisfaction rates reflect genuine choice rather than method limitations
- Partner/spousal consent is not a significant barrier to contraceptive access

Reflection questions:

- Does the 20% unmet need concentrate among specific populations (adolescents, rural women, unmarried women) who face additional gender-related access barriers?
- To what extent does male partner involvement—either supportive or restrictive—influence contraceptive uptake in Malawi?
- Are current family planning services designed to accommodate women with limited autonomy in household decision-making?

sections.heading: Antenatal care
sections.text:
Interpretation: The significant gap between first trimester ANC coverage (27.6%) and ANC 4+ visits (62.4%) suggests women are entering care late in pregnancy. This pattern may reflect gendered constraints including women's limited control over household resources for transport, time poverty due to domestic responsibilities, or cultural norms around pregnancy disclosure. Late ANC initiation also occurs due to limited pregnancy diagnosis options at both individual and health system level. Late ANC initiation reduces opportunities for early risk detection and birth preparedness.

Assumptions for team validation:

- Late ANC initiation is primarily driven by demand-side barriers rather than supply-side availability
- Women have agency to seek care independently once pregnancy is confirmed
- The ANC 4+ figure reflects the recommended contact schedule quality

Reflection questions:

- What gender-specific barriers (financial dependence, time constraints, need for permission) delay women's first ANC visit in Malawi?
- Are there cultural practices around pregnancy concealment that disproportionately affect women's early care-seeking?
- How do women's domestic and caregiving responsibilities influence their ability to attend multiple ANC visits?

sections.heading: Delivery and postnatal care
sections.text:
Interpretation: Malawi's high institutional delivery rate (95.2%) represents a significant achievement in ensuring women access skilled birth attendance. The C-section rate of 9.6% falls slightly below the WHO-recommended ranges (10-15%), suggesting somewhat appropriate access to emergency obstetric care without over-medicalization. Strong postnatal care coverage (84.1%) indicates continued engagement with the health system post-delivery. These figures suggest health system investments have successfully addressed major access barriers for facility-based care.

Assumptions for team validation:

- High institutional delivery rates reflect genuine access and quality rather than coercive policies
- The C-section rate is equitably distributed across wealth and geographic groups
- Postnatal care includes meaningful content addressing maternal and newborn health needs

Reflection questions:

- Does the high institutional delivery rate mask variations in quality or respectful maternity care practices?
- Is the C-section rate equitably available to women in rural areas facing obstetric emergencies?
- Does PNC adequately address women's own health needs, or does it focus predominantly on newborn care?

sections.heading: Equity
sections.text:
Interpretation: The 25 percentage-point urban/rural gap in institutional delivery reveals significant geographic inequity, likely reflecting rural women's compounded disadvantages including distance to facilities, transport costs, and limited infrastructure. The 15 percentage-point education gap demonstrates how women's educational attainment—itself shaped by gender norms—influences maternal health outcomes. Less-educated women may face greater barriers including limited health literacy, reduced autonomy, and economic constraints that intersect with gender-based inequities.

Assumptions for team validation:

- The urban/rural gap primarily reflects supply-side factors (facility availability) rather than demand-side preferences
- Educational attainment serves as a proxy for women's empowerment and decision-making capacity
- These gaps have remained stable and are not already being addressed by recent interventions

Reflection questions:

- For rural women who deliver outside institutions, what are the primary gendered barriers—distance, cost, permission, or preference for traditional care?
- How does low educational attainment intersect with other dimensions of marginalization (poverty, age, parity) to compound barriers for specific groups of women?
- Are existing programs specifically designed to reach women facing multiple intersecting disadvantages?

sections.heading: Suggested policy message options
sections.text:
Based on the data provided, the following illustrative policy messages are offered as starting points for country team discussion:

- Closing the unmet need gap: With 20% of women unable to access desired family planning despite 80.6% demand satisfaction, targeted interventions addressing gendered barriers—including partner engagement and adolescent-friendly services—could accelerate progress toward full reproductive autonomy.
- Early ANC as a gender equity priority: The 35 percentage-point gap between first trimester ANC (27.6%) and ANC 4+ coverage (62.4%) suggests women face early pregnancy barriers; addressing women's financial dependence and time poverty could improve early care initiation.
- Sustaining delivery gains while addressing quality: Malawi's 95.2% institutional delivery rate demonstrates strong access; the next frontier involves ensuring respectful, woman-centered care that upholds dignity and autonomy during childbirth.
- Rural women's access imperative: The 25 percentage-point urban/rural delivery gap indicates rural women face compounded geographic and gender barriers; community-based strategies and transport solutions could address these intersecting disadvantages.
- Education-sensitive approaches: The 15 percentage-point education gap in institutional delivery suggests less-educated women require tailored outreach that accounts for limited health literacy and potential constraints on autonomous decision-making.

These are illustrative examples intended to spark discussion. Country teams should validate for accuracy and relevance to current policy priorities, adapt language to local context, or develop alternative messages that better reflect their strategic objectives. Teams may select, combine, revise, or replace these options entirely.

sections.heading: The AI assistant in DataSuite
sections.text:
DataSuite's chat assistant works alongside the RMNCAH, Vaxx and Pooled apps. It is built to follow the guidance above:
it supports your analysis, and your team stays responsible for the interpretation.

sections.heading: What it knows
sections.text:
- Where you are. It knows which app page you are on, which charts and tabs are on screen, and the filters you have
  set, so you can ask "what does this chart show?" or "which page am I on?".
- Your dataset. It answers from the results your dataset has saved -- the same numbers the app shows -- not from
  estimates of its own. It can look at other levels too, for example which districts drive a change in a national
  indicator.
- This methodology. It explains results with the Countdown methodology on this site. When the methodology does not
  cover a question, it says so rather than filling the gap.

sections.heading: What it tells you
sections.text:
Every answer that uses the methodology or your data ends with its sources: the documentation sections it relied on,
as links, and the data it used -- a chart on screen, or a result saved in your dataset. When it calculates something
the app does not show, it says so.

sections.heading: What it can do
sections.text:
- Explain a chart or a page, and what the results mean.
- Break a change down by region or district.
- Build a report: one of the standard reports, or a custom one you then edit in the Reports page.
- Make a custom chart that is saved with your dataset and redraws when the data changes, like the app's own charts.
- Open another dataset in its own tab, so each dataset keeps its own conversation context.

sections.heading: What it will not do
sections.text:
- Change your dataset, except to save a report or a chart you asked for.
- Change what the app shows (go to another page, set filters) unless your setting allows it. The setting
  AI App Control has three choices: ask each time (the default), allow, or off.

sections.heading: Where its files are
sections.text:
The assistant keeps its files for an analysis next to your dataset, in the ai folder of the dataset's
<name>.shiny-workspace folder: the code it ran, conversation transcripts and the decisions it recorded. They stay
with the data they are about.

ai.summary: AI can support analysis and interpretation but must not replace the analyst's judgement: outputs must be reviewed, validated and adapted, and final interpretations, conclusions and recommendations stay grounded in human and subject-matter expertise and local context.
rules: AI can amplify: sharpening the question, surfacing data quality issues, pattern detection, structured comparisons, visual summaries, possible explanations, options and scenarios, counterarguments, refining messages (#)

AI must not replace: framing the question, judging data quality and fitness for use, deciding which patterns and comparisons are valid, choosing visualizations, judging explanations and causality, weighing options and owning decisions, stakeholder perspectives, ensuring messages are accurate and appropriate (#)
An effective prompt states its purpose, audience, geography, time and scope, interpretation guidance, output format and guardrails (#what-makes-an-effective-prompt)
Guardrails: stick to the data shown, flag uncertainty and data quality issues, avoid speculation beyond the evidence, note assumptions and inferences (#what-makes-an-effective-prompt)
Distinguish what the data shows (analysis) from what it may mean (interpretation), and state limitations, assumptions and uncertainty (#what-makes-an-effective-prompt)

The gender prompt uses only the data points supplied, and its output is a starting point with assumptions and reflective questions for country team review (#using-ai-prompts-to-support-gender-analysis-and-interpretation)
The DataSuite assistant answers from the dataset's saved results and this methodology, ends answers with its sources, and says when the methodology does not cover a question (#what-it-knows)
It changes what the app shows only as the AI App Control setting allows (ask, allow, off), and changes the dataset only to save a report or chart the user asked for (#what-it-will-not-do)
interpretation: The Malawi output and its policy messages are illustrative only, not findings or method (#example-of-an-ai-output-using-malawi-2025-cam-data)

sections.heading: Building apps for DataSuite
sections.text:
DataSuite runs R Shiny apps in its own tabs. An app comes to DataSuite inside an extension: the extension's
package.json describes the app, and DataSuite installs the app's R code, keeps it up to date and starts it when the
user opens a file.

This page is for people who write those apps. It covers what DataSuite expects so that an app installs cleanly on a
user's computer and keeps working as R packages change.

Users install nothing by hand: DataSuite needs R 4.1 or newer on the computer, and installs everything else the app
declares into its own R library. Whatever an app does not declare, DataSuite cannot install.

sections.heading: The short version
sections.text:
- Make the app an R package that exports run_app(). A plain app folder works too, but a package is easier to
  install, test and version.
- Declare every dependency in DESCRIPTION, each with a minimum version: dplyr (>= 1.1.4), never a bare dplyr.
- Never install packages while the app runs: no install.packages(), pak or remotes in the app's code.
- Version with semantic versioning, and write every change in NEWS.md.
- Release through the extension: a new extension version is what makes DataSuite update users' R packages.

The rest of this page explains each rule.

sections.heading: As an R package (recommended)
As a plain app folder
sections.text:
An app.R (or ui.R and server.R) in the folder named by location, with no package. DataSuite runs it with
shiny::runApp().

Put a DESCRIPTION file next to app.R that lists what the app uses, with minimum versions, in the same format a
package uses:

Depends: R (>= 4.1.0)
Imports:
    dplyr (>= 1.1.4),
    ggplot2 (>= 3.5.0),
    shiny (>= 1.8.0)

DataSuite does not read an app folder's DESCRIPTION yet: today a plain app gets its packages only when it fails
with "there is no package called ...", when DataSuite offers to install the missing package. Write the DESCRIPTION
now anyway -- it documents the app's needs, renv and rsconnect (Posit Connect) already read it, and DataSuite
will install from it.

sections.heading: 2. Declare dependencies
sections.text:
In DESCRIPTION:

Field | What goes there
Depends | R (>= 4.1.0)

-- the oldest R the app works with (DataSuite needs 4.1 or newer).
Imports | Every package the code needs,

each with a minimum version

.
Suggests | Optional features the code checks for with

requireNamespace()

(e.g. PDF export), also with minimum versions. DataSuite installs these for the app's own packages when it can, but never fails because one is missing.
Remotes | Packages that are not on CRAN, e.g.

owner/otherpkg

, so installs from GitHub work too.

sections.heading: Why every dependency needs a minimum version
sections.text:
DataSuite updates a CRAN package on a user's computer only when a DESCRIPTION asks for a newer version than the user
has. It never updates CRAN packages just because a newer one exists -- that would change packages under apps that
were never tested with them.

So with a bare dplyr, a user who has an old dplyr keeps it, and the first time the app calls a function newer than
their copy, it stops with "could not find function" or "unused argument". R CMD check does not catch this: it runs
against your own, newer library.

How to choose the minimum:

- The version that introduced the newest function or argument your code uses from that package (see the package's
  NEWS).
- When unsure, the version you develop and test with (packageVersion("dplyr")).
- Not a CRAN version released in the last day or two: Windows gets CRAN's prebuilt binaries, which can lag a release.
- Packages that come with R (base, stats, utils, graphics, grDevices, tools, methods) need no minimum: they come with
  R, so Depends: R (>= ...) covers them.

When you start using something newer from a package, raise its minimum in the same change.

sections.heading: Call functions explicitly
sections.text:
Use pkg::fun() or @importFrom pkg fun in package code, never library() or require(). That way R CMD check
tells you when something is used but not declared.

sections.heading: 3. Don't install at run time
sections.text:
Don't call install.packages(), pak::pkg_install(), remotes::install_*() or devtools::* from the app. DataSuite
installs what the app declares -- into its own library, in a separate R process, and only when no app tab has the
packages loaded (Windows can't replace a loaded package). An app that installs packages itself can break other apps
and fail on computers without the right permissions.

sections.heading: 4. Version numbers
sections.text:
Use semantic versioning for the package:

Change | Bump | Example
Breaks code or data that uses it: a renamed or removed function, changed arguments, a saved-file format that older versions can't read | major | 1.4.2 → 2.0.0
Adds something without breaking anything | minor | 1.4.2 → 1.5.0
Fixes only | patch | 1.4.2 → 1.4.3

Write every release in NEWS.md; for a major version, say what users or other packages must change.

The extension has its own version (in its package.json), bumped on the same rules for its own changes. An extension
release that only raises package.version is a patch.

sections.heading: 5. Release
sections.text:
- Update your development library to current CRAN (update.packages()), so you test what a new user would get.
- Run devtools::check(): 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 notes.
- Bump Version:, write NEWS.md, commit, tag vX.Y.Z and push. Wait for your repository (e.g. r-universe) to build
  it.
- If you publish several packages that depend on each other, release them in dependency order and wait for each
  build before releasing the next -- a package published before the version it requires fails to install.
- In the extension, raise package.version if users must have the new version, bump the extension's version and
  publish it.

sections.heading: How updates reach users
sections.text:
When | What DataSuite does
The extension is installed | Installs the app's package and everything it declares.
The extension is updated

(any new version) | Updates the app's package and every dependency from its own repositories to the newest version; installs or updates any CRAN package that is missing or older than a DESCRIPTION requires.
Before every launch | Checks the package is installed at

package.version

or newer; installs only if it isn't. Works offline once set up.
An app tab is open | Waits: updates run once the app's tabs are closed.
Offline | Keeps what is installed if it is new enough, and tries again later.

So publishing a new package version alone reaches new installs only (they get the newest); existing users get it
with the next extension release. That is deliberate: users only ever run combinations you released together.

sections.heading: Keeping an app working over time
sections.text:
Minimum versions protect against packages that are too old. They don't protect against a package's new
version breaking your app -- and apps outside CRAN get no warning when a CRAN package they use changes.

- Run R CMD check on a schedule against current CRAN, e.g. a weekly GitHub Actions workflow
  (r-lib/actions has ready-made ones). A breaking release then shows up as a
  failed run, usually before your users meet it.
- Don't pin exact versions or add upper limits (dplyr (< 1.2)): DataSuite only understands minimums, and upper limits
  conflict with other packages that need newer versions.

Planned in DataSuite: installing CRAN packages as of a date the app declares (a dated CRAN snapshot), so every user
gets exactly the versions the author tested with; a separate R library per extension, so one app's updates can't
change another's packages; and installing a plain app folder's dependencies from its DESCRIPTION. Following the
conventions on this page now means nothing changes for your app when they arrive.

sections.heading: Python apps
sections.text:
DataSuite also runs apps written with Shiny for Python, in the same tabs and with the
same restart, crash recovery and environment variables as R apps. Users need Python 3.10 or newer from
python.org (DataSuite finds it through the py launcher, the PATH or the
usual install folders, or the datasuite.pythonPath setting); DataSuite installs everything else.

The app's folder holds an app.py whose Shiny app object is named app:

from shiny import App, ui, render

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(ui.output_text("hello"))

def server(input, output, session):
    @render.text
    def hello():
        return "Hello"

app = App(app_ui, server)

and the extension marks it with "runtime": "python":

"shinyApps": [{
  "id": "myapp", "name": "My App", "location": "apps/myapp", "runtime": "python",
  "accepts": ["csv"],
  "package": { "name": "mypkg", "version": "1.2.0" }
}]

Dependencies go in a requirements.txt next to app.py, each with a minimum version, for the same reasons as
above:

pandas>=2.1
plotly>=5.18

A pyproject.toml with a [project] dependencies list works too (when both exist, requirements.txt is used; reading
pyproject.toml needs Python 3.11 or newer). Shiny for Python itself is always installed. package is optional: a
pip package the app comes from, with version its oldest supported version and index an extra package index to
look in besides PyPI; app.py then only imports the app, e.g. from mypkg.app import app.

DataSuite installs all of this into its own virtual environment, one per Python version
(<user data>/python/venv/<version>), never into the user's Python, with the same rules as R: when the extension is
installed or updated (the package is brought up to its newest version), a quick check before every launch that
downloads nothing when every requirement is met, and working offline once set up. If a running app imports a module
that isn't installed, DataSuite offers to install the pip package of the same name -- if the name differs (e.g.
sklearn is scikit-learn), list it in requirements.txt.

On Windows, keep paths short: the Python kernel can't open files whose full path is longer than 260 characters, so
a deeply nested app folder or package can fail to import.

sections.heading: What DataSuite gives a running app
sections.text:
DataSuite starts the app in a fresh R (or Python) session with these environment variables (Sys.getenv() in R,
os.environ in Python):

Variable | Value
CDSUITE_SHINY_ID | The app's

id

.
CDSUITE_SHINY_NAME | The app's

name

.
CDSUITE_SHINY_SELECTED_FILE | The file the user opened, if any.
CDSUITE_SHINY_WORKSPACE_DIR | A folder for the app's work on that file,

<file name>.shiny-workspace

next to it.
CDSUITE_SHINY_LOCALE | The display language, e.g.

en

,

fr

,

pt

.

Other shinyApps fields:

Field | Purpose
description

,

icon | Shown in menus, tooltips and the Start page (

icon

is a codicon id).
showOnStartPage | Also list the app on the Start page.
capabilities | requiresFile

,

canSelectFiles

,

canSelectFolders

,

canSelectMany

: what the file picker allows.
cache | { "file": "<stem>.rds" }

: the file the app saves its work to next to the data file. Opening the data file again opens the saved file.
aiModelRole | fast

,

balanced

or

reasoning

: the least capable AI model the app's analysis can use. While the app's tab is active, the chat's Auto model choice uses at least this.

sections.heading: Checklist before publishing
sections.text:
- The app runs from run_app() (package) or app.R (folder), with nothing sourced from outside it.
- Every package the code uses is in DESCRIPTION, with a minimum version.
- devtools::check() is clean, against an up-to-date library.
- No install.packages() or similar anywhere in the app.
- Version bumped and NEWS.md written.
- The package is built in its repository before the extension is published.
- The extension's package.version is raised if users need this version.

sections.heading: Advanced analysis
sections.text:
This page applies to the RMNCAH app only.

Three analyses go beyond the basic coverage charts: Bayesian Analysis, Continuum of Care and FPET FP Projection. They build on the adjusted data and the denominators you selected, so finish Data preparation and Denominators first. Methods: Bayesian modeling approach and National coverage.

sections.heading: Bayesian Analysis
sections.text:
Purpose. Combine survey data and routine facility data into one estimate per year, with a range of uncertainty and a short-term forecast. How the model uses each source: Bayesian modeling approach > How are survey data used? and How are routine data used?

When to use it. See Bayesian modeling approach > Why it matters.

There are two entries in the Bayesian Analysis group of the sidebar: National Analysis and Sub-National Analysis (regions).

sections.heading: Open Bayesian Analysis
sections.text: Choose National Analysis or Sub-National Analysis.

sections.heading: Pick an indicator tab
sections.text: ANC 4 Visits, ANC 1st Trimester, Institutional Deliveries, Measles 1 or Pentavalent 3. The model is defined for these five indicators.

sections.heading: Read the chart
sections.text:
The title is Bayesian Coverage Model Estimates followed by the indicator, and the source note reads Survey Data & DHIS2 Routine Data. The central line is the best estimate; the band is the uncertainty range. Use Download Plot and Download Data in the toolbar.

Bayesian ANC4 estimates at national level

Bayesian ANC4 estimates by region

How to interpret. See Bayesian modeling approach > Reading the estimates and the illustrative examples.

sections.heading: Continuum of Care
sections.text:
Purpose. Follow coverage along the care pathway and see where women and children drop out.

Where. National Analysis, Continuum of Care in the sidebar. The page has two cards, both titled National Coverage & Continuum, each with the tabs Maternal Continuum and Child Continuum.

- Top card, continuum profile. National continuum-of-care profile: the latest facility value, the latest survey value and, where relevant, the WUENIC value for each step of the selected pathway, for example ANC 1st Trimester, ANC 4 Visits, Institutional Deliveries and PNC within 48 hours for the maternal continuum, or Pentavalent 3 and Measles 1 for the child continuum.
- Bottom card, continuum heatmap. Subnational continuum heatmap: the same steps for each Admin 1 region. Read across a row to see one region, down a column to see one indicator. Red cells are low coverage, yellow intermediate and green high.

The page can generate the national coverage report with Generate Report.

Continuum of care profile

Maternal continuum heatmap by region

How to interpret. See National coverage > Interpreting the maternal continuum, Interpreting the child continuum and Continuum of care at subnational level.

sections.heading: FPET FP Projection
sections.text:
Purpose. Show family planning trends for currently married women aged 15 to 49, from the Family Planning Estimation Tool (FPET, Track20).

Where. It is the FP Projection tab on National Coverage and on Sub-National Coverage.

The chart title is Family planning among currently married women 15-49 years. It draws two indicators: Prevalence of Modern Methods (mCPR) and Demand Satisfied with a Modern Method.

FPET projection

How to interpret. See National coverage > Family planning projections; where the data come from: Family planning.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
- Pitfalls in using the Bayesian estimates: Bayesian modeling approach > Common pitfalls.
- Pitfalls in reading the FP Projection and the continuum heatmap: National coverage > Common pitfalls.

ai.summary: Bayesian Analysis, Continuum of Care and FPET FP Projection go beyond the basic coverage charts. They build on the adjusted data and the selected denominators, so Data preparation and Denominators come first.
rules: Reading the FP Projection and the continuum heatmap, and their pitfalls, is in National coverage (/en/docs/methodology/coverage/)
How the Bayesian model uses surveys and routine data, and how to read its estimates, is in Bayesian coverage (/en/docs/methodology/bayesian-coverage/)
Methods are in Bayesian coverage (/en/docs/methodology/bayesian-coverage/)
Coverage methods are in National coverage (/en/docs/methodology/coverage/)
interpretation: Bayesian Analysis combines survey and routine data into one estimate per year with an uncertainty band and a short forecast; available for ANC 4 Visits, ANC 1st Trimester, Institutional Deliveries, Measles 1 and Pentavalent 3 (#pick-an-indicator-tab)
Bayesian chart: the central line is the best estimate and the band the uncertainty range, with Download Plot and Download Data (#read-the-chart)
Continuum of Care: a national profile (facility, survey and WUENIC values per step) and a heatmap by Admin 1 region, for the Maternal and Child continuum (#continuum-of-care)

sections.text:
This page applies to the RMNCAH app only.

sections.heading: Coverage, equity and targets
sections.text:
These four pages sit in the National Analysis group of the sidebar: National Coverage, Coverage Target, National Inequality (routine data) and Equity Assessment (survey data). All of them need Data Adjustment to have been run (adjusted data) and use the denominators chosen on Denominator Selection. Sub-national versions are in Sub-national analysis. Methods are in National coverage and Equity assessment.

[RMNCAH] The pages use the maternal and vaccination denominators chosen on Denominator Selection.

[Vaxx] Under National Inequality the Vaxx app has two pages: Routine Data (inequality between regions) and Survey Data (the Equity Assessment). All pages use the vaccination denominator you chose in Denominators.

sections.heading: Indicators available
sections.text:
Each page shows a strip of tabs, one indicator per tab, and most strips end with a tab for any other indicator.

[RMNCAH] The default indicator tabs are ANC 4 Visits, Institutional Live Births, Low Birth Weight, Pentavalent 3 and Measles 1 (National Coverage also has FP Projection). The Custom tab covers any other indicator.

[Vaxx] Most tab strips end with a Custom Check tab that opens an Indicator selector listing every Vaxx analysis indicator:

- ANC 1, Institutional Deliveries and Institutional Live Births.
- BCG, IPV 1 and 2, Measles 1 and 2, OPV 1 to 3, Pentavalent 1 to 3, PCV 1 to 3, Rotavirus 1 and 2.
- Dropout: Penta 1 to Penta 3, Penta 1 to Measles 1, Penta 3 to Measles 1, Measles 1 to Measles 2.
- Zero-dose and Under-vaccinated.

What dropout, zero-dose and under-vaccinated measure: National coverage > Immunization.

sections.heading: National Coverage
sections.text:
Purpose. Compare facility-based (DHIS2) coverage with survey and WUENIC estimates of national coverage for each indicator.

When to use it. After denominators are chosen, to judge whether facility trends are believable.

sections.heading: Open National Coverage
sections.text:
[RMNCAH] There are no filters. The page uses the national level and the denominators you selected.

[Vaxx] It is the first page of the National Analysis section.

sections.heading: Pick an indicator tab
sections.text:
[RMNCAH] Tabs: ANC 4 Visits, Institutional Live Births, Low Birth Weight, Pentavalent 3, Measles 1, FP Projection (see Advanced analysis) and Custom for any other indicator.

[Vaxx] Choose a headline indicator, or Custom Check for any other.

sections.heading: Read the chart
sections.text: The chart is titled "National ... Coverage Estimates" and plots by year the DHIS2 estimate, the WUENIC estimate and the Survey estimate with its 95% CI, from 2010. The caption names the denominator that the DHIS2 values use.

sections.heading: Use the chart tools
sections.text:
Each chart has a toolbar to edit labels, change view or style, download the image (Download Plot) and download the data (Download Data). See Exports, reports and AI.

National coverage

sections.heading: How to interpret National Coverage
sections.text: What agreement or a gap between the lines means: National coverage > Interpreting the national trend. To follow up a gap, return to data quality and denominators.

sections.heading: Coverage Target
sections.text:
Purpose. Show the percentage of regions or districts (sub-national units) that reach a global coverage target, by year.

Filter. Admin Level (Admin 1 or Admin 2).

The chart title states the rule or threshold that was applied, for example the percentage of units meeting the target, and the bars show the percentage of units meeting it by year and indicator. The thresholds applied to regions and districts are in Subnational analysis > Target values.

[RMNCAH] Tabs are ANC 4 Visits, Institutional Live Births and Vaccine (BCG, Pentavalent 3 and Measles 1). Dropout targets are in the Vaxx app only.

Below the chart a table, Target Rate by Region (Admin 1) or Districts Meeting the Coverage Target (Admin 2), lists the units that reach the target for the indicator you choose in the This table only control.

[Vaxx] Two tabs:

Tab | Indicators
Vaccine | BCG, Pentavalent 3, Measles 1
Dropout | Penta 1 to Penta 3, Penta 3 to Measles 1

The table below the chart (Target Rate by Region at Admin 1, Districts Meeting the Coverage Target for Admin 2) lists the units that reach the vaccine threshold for the indicator and year chosen in its own selectors. It can be downloaded as an Excel file.

The same page for regions and districts is described under Sub-national analysis. Read the chart title for the direction of the rule (for dropout, lower is better). How to read the percentages: Subnational analysis > Global coverage targets.

Coverage against targets

sections.heading: National Inequality (routine data)
sections.text:
Purpose. See how much regions differ from the national figure, using facility data.

The card National Inequality (in the Vaxx app, the Routine Data page) has one tab per default indicator plus the Custom (Custom Check) tab, as above. Each chart shows coverage in every Admin 1 region by year (subtitle "Subnational unit: admin 1 level"): each dot is an Admin 1 region and the line is National Coverage. How to read the spread: Subnational analysis > Inequality. Investigate the weak areas in Sub-national analysis.

[RMNCAH] Tabs: ANC 4 Visits, Institutional Live Births, Low Birth Weight, Pentavalent 3, Measles 1 and Custom.

[Vaxx] Tabs and the Custom Check tab as above.

Under it, choose Select Years and a Palette (Greens, Blues, Reds or Purples) for the Sub-National Mapping card, which maps the coverage of each region for the selected years. In the Vaxx app each tab of the mapping card draws a map titled "Distribution of ... by Regions" from DHIS2 data, and the map follows the tab selected in the inequality card.

National inequality

sections.heading: Equity Assessment (survey data)
sections.text:
Purpose. Show inequality between population groups (household groups), using household survey data from the survey files loaded in the wizard.

When to use it. When survey files were loaded (or the built-in ones cover your country) and you want to know who is being left behind. In the Vaxx app this is the Survey Data page under National Inequality.

sections.heading: Choose the Equity Type
sections.text: Area (Rural, Urban), Maternal Education (No education, Primary, Secondary or higher) or Wealth Quintile.

sections.heading: Choose the indicator
sections.text:
[RMNCAH] ANC 4 Visits, Institutional Live Births, Low Birth Weight, Pentavalent 3, Measles 1 or Custom.

[Vaxx] Tabs are Pentavalent 3, Measles 1, and the dropouts Penta 1 to Penta 3 and Penta 3 to Measles 1, plus Custom Check.

sections.heading: Read the equiplot
sections.text:
The chart is titled "Inequalities in ... coverage by ..." and shows coverage for each group. How to read it: Equity assessment > Interpretation of equiplots.

[RMNCAH] Each group has its own line over time, with the national trend for comparison. Generate Report opens the national inequality report.

[Vaxx] If a survey file was not uploaded, the built-in reference data are used. Upload the country's files in the Load Data wizard for a real assessment.

Equity by area of residence

Equity by wealth quintile

Equity by maternal education

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
- The equity pages rely on the survey files and the survey year from Load Data.
- Coverage and target pages change when you change the denominator. Record which denominator a result used (the chart caption shows it).

Pitfalls in reading these results: National coverage > Interpreting the national trend and Common pitfalls; Subnational analysis > Inequality; Equity assessment > Common pitfalls.

Next: Sub-national analysis.

All need adjusted data and use the denominators chosen on Denominator Selection (one vaccination denominator in Vaxx).
options: Vaxx Custom Check indicators: ANC 1, institutional deliveries and live births; BCG, IPV, Measles, OPV, Pentavalent, PCV, Rotavirus doses; dropout Penta 1 to Penta 3, Penta 1 to Measles 1, Penta 3 to Measles 1, Measles 1 to Measles 2; Zero-dose and Under-vaccinated (#indicators-available)
Coverage Target tabs: ANC 4 Visits, Institutional Live Births and Vaccine (RMNCAH); Vaccine and Dropout (Vaxx); filter Admin Level (Admin 1 or Admin 2) (#coverage-target)
rules: Record which denominator a result used (the chart caption shows it); the equity pages rely on the survey files and survey year from Load Data (#common-pitfalls)
Coverage and dropout definitions and how to read National Coverage are in National coverage (/en/docs/methodology/coverage#interpreting-the-national-trend)
The target thresholds are in Subnational analysis (/en/docs/methodology/subnational#target-values)
How to read inequality and targets is in Subnational analysis (/en/docs/methodology/subnational#reading-inequality)
Equity methods and how to read equiplots are in Equity analysis (/en/docs/methodology/equity#interpretation-of-equiplots)
interpretation: National Coverage: DHIS2, WUENIC and Survey (95% CI) lines per indicator tab; the caption names the denominator (#read-the-chart)
National Inequality: each dot is an Admin 1 region by year, the line is national coverage (#national-inequality-routine-data)
Equity Assessment: an equiplot per Equity Type (Area, Maternal Education, Wealth Quintile), coverage for each group (#read-the-equiplot)
Coverage Target: bars show the percentage of units meeting the target by year and indicator; the chart title states the rule applied (#coverage-target)

sections.heading: Data preparation
sections.text:
Data preparation turns the reported numbers into an analysis-ready dataset, the dataset used for coverage. It has three pages: Remove Years, Data Adjustment and Data Adjustment Changes (in the RMNCAH app they are in the Data quality section). The method, formulas and business rules are in Data adjustment.

Adjusting the data is required. Running the adjustment is what unlocks the later pages: in the RMNCAH app the Denominators and Analysis pages; in the Vaxx app denominators, coverage, inequality, targets and Reports stay unavailable until you run Adjust Data at least once.

sections.heading: Remove Years
sections.text:
Purpose. Leave out years whose data cannot be relied on.

When to use it. When to remove a year, and when to keep it: Data adjustment > Remove years.

sections.heading: Open Remove Years
sections.text: In the RMNCAH app it is under Data quality in the sidebar. Decide from the data quality pages first.

sections.heading: Select Years to Remove
sections.text: In Select Years to Remove, the chips list the years present in the data. Select one or more.

sections.heading: Press Confirm Removal
sections.text:
The message changes from No years have been removed yet to Data for the following years has been removed, followed by the years. To bring a year back (restore years), deselect it or clear the selection and confirm again.

Remove years

Removal happens before adjustment. If you have already adjusted, run Adjust Data again after changing the removed years.

sections.heading: Data Adjustment
sections.text:
Purpose. Correct for incomplete reporting (missing reports) and extreme outliers. How missing values, outliers and the K-factor are handled: Data adjustment > Method.

The page has two cards: K-Factors (Adjustment Factors) and the adjustment card with Adjust Data, which applies the corrections to the current dataset.

sections.heading: Choose the K-Factors
sections.text:
[RMNCAH] The card K-Factors (Adjustment Factors) has four selectors: ANC K-Factor, Delivery K-Factor, Vaccines K-Factor and OPD K-Factor. Each offers 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1. What each value assumes and how to choose: Data adjustment > Configuring the k-factor.

[Vaxx] The card K-Factors (Adjustment Factors) has an ANC K-Factor, a Delivery K-Factor and a Vaccines K-Factor, each a choice of 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 or 1. The page shows the values stored in the dataset. Pick a value for each of the three factors; the starting value, the guidebook's default and how to choose: Data adjustment > Configuring the k-factor.

sections.heading: Press Adjust Data
sections.text:
[RMNCAH] The message goes from Dataset not adjusted to Adjusting ... and then Data Adjusted. Do this even if you keep every factor at 0, because it is what unlocks the analysis pages.

[Vaxx] Choose Adjust Data and wait for "Data Adjusted". The status box shows "Not adjusted yet", then "Adjusting ...", then "Data Adjusted".

sections.heading: Download the result if you need it
sections.text: Once adjusted, Download Adjusted Dataset saves the adjusted master dataset as a .dta file (master_adj_dataset.dta).

sections.heading: Review the changes
sections.text:
Open Data Adjustment Changes.

Changing the K-factors or the removed years discards the adjusted dataset. Press Adjust Data again, otherwise the analysis pages will not reflect your change. If the adjustment fails, the message shows the reason.

How a district-month with reporting below 75% (or missing) is handled: Data adjustment > Critical data threshold rules.

K-factor selection

sections.heading: Data Adjustment Changes
sections.text:
Purpose. See what the adjustment did to each indicator.

How to read it. The card Visualize effects of changes has one tab per indicator. Each chart compares the number of events (of the indicator) before and after adjustment for completeness and outliers, by year.

[RMNCAH] Tabs are Institutional Deliveries, Institutional Live Births, Pentavalent 1, ANC 1 and OPD Under 5 Years, plus a Custom tab for any other indicator. Use Download Plot and Download Data on the toolbar. Generate Report opens the adjustment report.

[Vaxx] Tabs are Institutional Live Births, BCG, Pentavalent 1 and Measles 1, plus a Custom Check tab with an indicator selector.

If the data have not been adjusted, the chart uses a K-factor of 0 for every service, so it shows only what outlier and missing value handling do.

Before and after adjustment

sections.heading: How to interpret the results
sections.text: How to read the before-and-after charts: Data adjustment > Adjustment outputs. What to report: Data adjustment > Report.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
- Changing K-factors, removed years or the performance threshold affects every downstream page. Re-run Adjust Data and re-check denominators afterwards.
- Reports and pooled caches should be built from adjusted data. See Pooled App.

Pitfalls in choosing the K-factors and removing years, and which indicators are not adjusted: Data adjustment > Common pitfalls.

Next: Denominators.

ai.summary: Data preparation turns the reported numbers into an analysis-ready dataset with three pages: Remove Years, Data Adjustment and Data Adjustment Changes. Adjusting is required: running Adjust Data unlocks the later pages (RMNCAH: Denominators and Analysis; Vaxx: denominators, coverage, inequality, targets and Reports).
options: K-Factors, each 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 or 1: ANC, Delivery, Vaccines and OPD in RMNCAH; ANC, Delivery and Vaccines in Vaxx (#choose-the-k-factors)
steps: Remove Years: confirm on the data quality pages that a year is unusable, select it and press Confirm Removal; deselect and confirm again to bring one back (#press-confirm-removal)
Data Adjustment: choose the K-Factors and press Adjust Data until it says Data Adjusted (#press-adjust-data)
Data Adjustment Changes: compare numbers before and after adjustment for each indicator (#data-adjustment-changes)
rules: Removal happens before adjustment; after changing the removed years, press Adjust Data again (#remove-years)
The page shows the K-factors stored in the dataset (#choose-the-k-factors)
RMNCAH: press Adjust Data even with every factor at 0; it unlocks the analysis pages (#press-adjust-data)
Changing K-factors, removed years or the threshold discards the adjustment until Adjust Data is pressed again; then re-check denominators (#common-pitfalls)
Reports and pooled caches should be built from adjusted data (#common-pitfalls)
The method, formulas and business rules (what each K-factor assumes, when to remove a year, the 75% rule, outliers and missing values) are in Data adjustment (/en/docs/methodology/data-adjustment/)

How to read the before-and-after comparison, what to report, and the pitfalls in choosing K and removing years are in Data adjustment > Interpretation (/en/docs/methodology/data-adjustment/#interpretation)
interpretation: Data Adjustment Changes: one tab per indicator; each chart compares the number of events before and after adjustment for completeness and outliers, by year; in Vaxx, before any adjustment the chart uses a K-factor of 0 for every service (#data-adjustment-changes)

sections.heading: Data quality
sections.text: Data quality is the first analysis stage. It answers one question before any coverage is calculated: can the facility data be trusted? Five pages, under Data quality in the RMNCAH app and Data Quality Assessment in the Vaxx app, show how complete, plausible and consistent the routine data are. Their results decide whether you remove years and how you adjust the data in Data preparation. The method is explained in Data quality assessment.

sections.heading: When to use it
sections.text: Use these pages right after loading the data, and again whenever you upload a corrected file. Load Data must be finished first; these pages do not need Data Adjustment. Review them in this order: Reporting Rate, Outlier Detection, Data Missingness, Internal Consistency, Overall Data Quality Score. Then move on to Data preparation.

sections.heading: Common filters
sections.text:
[RMNCAH] Most pages have an Indicator chip, an Admin Level chip (Admin 1 or Admin 2) and, when Admin 1 is selected, a region chip with Select All to focus on one region. The Reporting Rate page adds a Performance Threshold (see Reporting Rate).

[Vaxx] - Indicator: pick what to assess. Outlier, missingness and consistency pages list all Vaxx indicators (ANC1, Institutional Deliveries, Institutional Live Births, BCG, IPV 1-2, Measles 1-2, OPV 1-3, Pentavalent 1-3, PCV 1-3, Rotavirus 1-2). Reporting Rate uses three service groups: ANC, Institutional Delivery and Vaccination.
- Admin Level: Admin 1 (regions) or Admin 2 (districts). A region selector lets you focus on the districts of one region.
- Performance Threshold (Reporting Rate only): a percentage, 90 by default with quick picks of 70, 80, 90 and 95. It is saved in the dataset and reused by the Overall Data Quality Score.

sections.heading: Open the page from the sidebar
sections.text: The pages are under Data quality (RMNCAH) or Data Quality Assessment (Vaxx). Load Data must be finished first.

sections.heading: Set the filters
sections.text: Choose the indicator, the admin level and, if you want, a region, as described in Common filters.

sections.heading: Read the chart, then the table below it
sections.text: Charts show the pattern. Tables list the districts and months behind it. Use the toolbar of a card for Download Plot (PNG) and Download Data (Excel), and the This table only year selector for tables.

sections.heading: Reporting Rate
sections.text: Shows how completely facilities reported, by service, year and area.

sections.heading: Choose the service, threshold and admin level
sections.text:
[RMNCAH] - Indicator: ANC, Institutional Delivery, Vaccination, OPD.
- Performance Threshold: default 90%; quick picks 70, 80, 90, 95.
- Admin Level.

[Vaxx] Select ANC, Institutional Delivery or Vaccination, set the threshold, then the admin level.

sections.heading: Read Sub-National Reporting Rate
sections.text: The Heat Map tab shows the reporting rate of the selected service for each area and year. The Bar Graph tab shows the rate by year.

sections.heading: Read the National Reporting Rate card and the table
sections.text:
The National Reporting Rate card (in the RMNCAH app, District Reporting Rate in a region when a region is chosen) shows the percentage of districts whose reporting rate is below the threshold (low reporting), one panel per service, by year. Sub-National Units with Low Reporting lists the districts or regions below the threshold for the selected year and service.

What the reporting rate measures and how to read it: Data quality > Reporting completeness and Reporting rates.

The Performance Threshold you set here is stored in the dataset and reused by the Overall Data Quality Score and, in the RMNCAH app, the Service Utilization DQA.

Sub-national reporting rate heat map

sections.heading: Outlier Detection
sections.text:
Finds extreme monthly values that may be data entry errors. What counts as an extreme outlier: Data quality > Outlier detection.

- Filters: Indicator and Admin Level.
- Indicators with Outliers card: tabs Heat Map (percent of monthly values that are not outliers, by area and year), Indicator Bar Graph (by year and indicator) and Region Bar Graph (by year and region).
- Sub-National Units with Extreme Outliers: every flagged district and month, in a table of year, month, area, reported value, median and MAD. Pick the year with the This table only control.
- Sub-National Trends: pick a region and read the month-by-month plot for the selected year: the reported value against the median, the outlier bounds (plus or minus 5 MAD) and the outliers.

How to read it (the expected share of values free of outliers, campaigns): Data quality > Outliers.

Outlier detection heat map

sections.heading: Data Missingness
sections.text:
Shows which indicators and areas have missing reports.

- Filters: Indicator (with Select All) and Admin Level.
- Indicators with Missing Data: tabs Heat Map (percent of missing reports by year and area), Complete Indicators (percent of districts with complete data for the indicator) and Missing Indicators by Region (trend in completeness by region).
- Sub-National Units with Missing Data: a table of the districts with gaps (incomplete data) for the selected indicator and year.

How missing values are measured and handled: Data quality > Data missingness.

Data missingness heat map

sections.heading: Internal Consistency
sections.text:
Checks that related indicators move together and agree over time. Two cards are shown: Ratio Plots and Consistency Checks. The expected ratios and the range a district must fall in: Data quality > Internal consistency. How to read the plots: Data quality > Consistency and ratios.

[RMNCAH] - Ratio Plots: the yearly ratios ANC1 / Penta1 and Penta1 / Penta3 against the expected ratio. Expected ratios come from the survey coverage values entered in National Rates.
- Consistency Checks: tabs ANC1 and Penta1, Penta1 and Penta3 and Custom Check (choose an X axis and a Y axis). Each dot is a district, shown with a Linear fit and a Diagonal.

Ratio plots

[Vaxx] - Ratio Plots: ratios ANC1 / Penta1, Penta1 / Penta3 and OPV1 / OPV3 by year, compared with the expected ratios.
- Consistency Checks: tabs ANC1 and Penta1, Penta1 and Penta3, OPV1 and OPV3, IPV1 and IPV2, and Custom Check where you choose the X and Y indicators. Each plot draws one point per district and year, with a linear fit and a diagonal.

Consistency checks between ANC1 and Penta1

sections.heading: Overall Data Quality Score
sections.text:
One annual score across all checks: one table per year, with a region filter to see a single Admin 1 area, or the national level. How the score is computed: Data quality > Overall quality score.

[RMNCAH] Block | Rows
1. Completeness | % of expected monthly facility reports (national); % of districts at or above the threshold; % of districts with no missing values for the 4 forms
2. Extreme outliers | % of monthly values that are not extreme outliers; % of districts with no extreme outliers
3. Consistency | Ratios ANC1 / Penta1 and Penta1 / Penta3; % of districts within the expected range

The last row is the Annual data quality score. Use Download Plot and Download Data. Generate Report opens the data quality report.

[Vaxx] The table has three blocks:

- Completeness of monthly facility reporting (mean of ANC, delivery, immunization): percent of expected monthly reports nationally, and percent of districts with completeness at or above the threshold, and percent of districts with no missing values (mean for common vaccines).
- Extreme outliers: percent of monthly values that are not extreme outliers, and percent of districts with no extreme outliers in the year.
- Consistency of annual reporting: the three ratios and the percent of districts with ANC1/Penta1, Penta1/Penta3 and OPV1/OPV3 in the expected range.

The last row is the Annual data quality score. Use the two download buttons on the card to save the plot and the data.

Overall data quality score

sections.heading: Interpretation and pitfalls
sections.text:
How to read the results, and what to watch for before you remove years or adjust: Data quality > Interpretation, including its Common pitfalls.

Next: Data preparation.

ai.summary: The five data quality pages (Data quality in the RMNCAH app, Data Quality Assessment in the Vaxx app) answer whether the facility data can be trusted before any coverage is calculated; their results decide whether to remove years and how to adjust. Review them after loading, in order: Reporting Rate, Outlier Detection, Data Missingness, Internal Consistency, Overall Data Quality Score.
rules: Performance Threshold defaults to 90% (quick picks 70, 80, 90, 95), is stored in the dataset and reused by the Overall Data Quality Score and, in RMNCAH, the Service Utilization DQA (#reporting-rate)
RMNCAH: the expected ratios in the Ratio Plots use the survey coverage values entered in National Rates (#internal-consistency)
The method (the outlier test, the expected ratios and district range, the score's formula) is in Data quality assessment (/en/docs/methodology/data-quality/)
How to read the results, and the pitfalls in interpreting them, are in Data quality assessment > Interpretation (/en/docs/methodology/data-quality/#interpretation)
interpretation: Reporting Rate: Sub-National Reporting Rate (Heat Map, Bar Graph), National Reporting Rate (percent of districts below the threshold) and Sub-National Units with Low Reporting (#reporting-rate)
Outlier Detection: Indicators with Outliers (Heat Map, Indicator Bar Graph, Region Bar Graph), Sub-National Units with Extreme Outliers, Sub-National Trends (#outlier-detection)
Data Missingness: Indicators with Missing Data (Heat Map, Complete Indicators, Missing Indicators by Region) and Sub-National Units with Missing Data (#data-missingness)

Internal Consistency: Ratio Plots (ANC1/Penta1, Penta1/Penta3, and OPV1/OPV3 in Vaxx, against the expected ratio) and Consistency Checks (one point per district, with a linear fit and a diagonal) (#internal-consistency)
Overall Data Quality Score: completeness, extreme outliers and consistency blocks; the last row is the Annual data quality score (#overall-data-quality-score)

sections.heading: Denominators
sections.text:
Coverage is the number of people who received a service divided by the number who needed it; the denominator has to be estimated (see Denominators > Service coverage). The Denominators section has two pages, Denominator Assessment and Denominator Selection. The method is described in Denominator assessment and selection.

[RMNCAH] Both pages unlock after Data preparation.

[Vaxx] The Denominator Assessment page is labelled Population Trend in the menu. Both pages need adjusted data.

sections.heading: When to use it
sections.text: Use these pages after adjustment and before reading any coverage result. Repeat them if you change the adjustment or the survey inputs. Denominator Assessment comes first, before Denominator Selection.

sections.heading: Denominator options
sections.text:
The UN projection of live births is shown in the comparison charts only; it is not one of the choices in the selectors. The other options are:

[RMNCAH] The Maternal denominator and Vaccination denominator selectors offer the other five options.

Option in the app | Id in the data | Meaning
UN projections | un | UN projection of live births (national only)
DHIS2 projections | dhis2 | DHIS2 projection of live births
ANC1-derived | anc1 | Derived each year from women attending a first antenatal visit
Penta1-derived | penta1 | Derived each year from children receiving the first pentavalent dose
ANC1 population growth | anc1derived | The survey year's ANC1-derived value, carried to other years with population growth
Penta1 population growth | penta1derived | The survey year's Penta1-derived value, carried to other years with population growth

The ids ending in derived are the population-growth options, not the "-derived" ones: see the Data dictionary.

[Vaxx] The Vaccination denominator chip offers these options.

Option | Id in the data | Idea
DHIS2 projections | dhis2 | The population projected in the DHIS2 data (live births, total births, total population or under 1, per the Select Best Population setting).
ANC1-derived | anc1 | Denominator derived each year from ANC-1 service utilization.
Penta1-derived | penta1 | Denominator derived each year from Penta-1 immunization.
ANC1 population growth, Penta1 population growth | anc1derived

,

penta1derived | The survey year's ANC-1 or Penta-1 derivation, carried to other years with annual population growth.

The UN projection is also plotted on the charts for comparison, but it is not one of the choices in the chip.

What each option is, and how the derived populations are computed from the survey rates: Denominators > Denominator options and Computing the derived denominators.

sections.heading: Denominator Assessment
sections.text: Purpose. Compare population trends across the available sources and decide which population indicator is consistent between the UN and DHIS2 projections (what that choice drives: Denominators > Population trend comparison).

sections.heading: Open Denominator Assessment
sections.text: It is the first page of the Denominators section (Population Trend in the Vaxx app).

sections.heading: Compare the three tabs
sections.text: The card Population Comparison has the tabs Population, Births and Under 1. Each plots the UN projection against the DHIS2 projection in thousands, by year. The Births tab shows DHIS2 live births and DHIS2 total births.

sections.heading: Select Best Population
sections.text:
In the filter bar choose the population source that is most consistent with the UN: Live births (DHIS2), Total births (DHIS2), Total population (DHIS2) or Under 1 year (DHIS2).

How to choose, and what gaps or breaks between the lines mean: Denominators > Population trend comparison and Reading the population trends.

Population comparison between UN and DHIS2

sections.heading: Denominator Selection
sections.text:
Purpose. Compare coverage under each denominator option and choose the best denominator. The choice is what the rest of the analysis uses; it appears afterwards in the Denominator row (the denominator chip) of every analysis page.

[RMNCAH] Choose the best denominator for vaccination indicators and for maternal indicators.

Filters. Maternal denominator, Vaccination denominator and Admin Level (National, Admin 1 or Admin 2, with a region chip). The two denominator choices are what the rest of the analysis uses.

[Vaxx] Choose one vaccination denominator. Admin Level (National, Admin 1, Admin 2) and the region selector are used on the trend card.

Three cards support the decision:

sections.heading: Read the survey comparison (National Coverage)
sections.text:
[RMNCAH] For each indicator tab (Institutional Live Births and Pentavalent 3) the bars show facility-based coverage in the survey year under each denominator, compared with the national survey coverage.

[Vaxx] The National Coverage card has tabs Institutional Live Births, BCG, Pentavalent 3 and Measles 1. Each chart shows the facility-based coverage from DHIS2 under each denominator, next to the national survey coverage for the survey year.

How to read it: Denominators > Denominator selection examination (a).

If survey estimates are missing, the card shows No coverage to show yet and a Go to Load Data button. Add the survey values in the National Rates step.

sections.heading: Check the regional pattern (Subnational Derived Coverage)
sections.text:
Subnational Derived Coverage compares coverage by region and denominator in the survey year. How to read it: Denominators > Denominator selection examination (b).

In the Vaxx app its tabs are Pentavalent 1, Pentavalent 3 and Measles 1.

sections.heading: Check the trend (Population Trend)
sections.text:
The Population Trend card (on this page it means coverage over time) shows national coverage over time, or coverage for the selected area, for each denominator, including the UN population in the Vaxx app. Use the Admin Level filter (National, Admin 1, Admin 2) and the region selector to look at one area. How to read it: Denominators > Denominator selection examination (c).

In the Vaxx app its tabs are Pentavalent 1, Pentavalent 3 and Measles 1.

sections.heading: Choose the denominator
sections.text:
[RMNCAH] Set the Maternal denominator and the Vaccination denominator, and record why in your notes. How to combine the three views: Denominators > Final selection and synthesis.

[Vaxx] Set the Vaccination denominator chip. Options are DHIS2 projections, ANC1-derived, Penta1-derived, Penta1 population growth and ANC1 population growth. The choice is saved in the dataset and used by every coverage, inequality and target page. The Vaxx App has one vaccination denominator, with no separate maternal one. How to combine the three views: Denominators > Final selection and synthesis.

Best denominator selection

National coverage over time by denominator

sections.heading: How to interpret the results
sections.text:
What makes a denominator the best one, and what to watch for: Denominators > Final selection and synthesis and Common pitfalls.

- The denominator label appears on every analysis page (in the Vaxx app, the vaccination denominator chip). If results look odd, check it first, then return to Data quality.

The denominator you select changes every coverage, inequality, target, mortality and health system chart. If you change it later, review the pages that depend on it and regenerate any exported figures.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
- Missing survey coverage values in Load Data, which leaves the survey comparison empty.
- Setting the denominator again for each chart: it is set once, on Denominator Selection, for the whole analysis. For pitfalls in choosing it, see Denominators > Common pitfalls.

Next: Coverage, equity and targets.

ai.summary: Coverage divides a facility numerator by an estimated denominator, so the denominator matters as much as data quality. Denominator Assessment (Population Trend in Vaxx) picks the DHIS2 population series most consistent with the UN projection; Denominator Selection compares coverage under each option and records the denominator the whole analysis uses: a maternal and a vaccination one in RMNCAH, one vaccination denominator in Vaxx.

Vaxx: DHIS2 projections, ANC1-derived, Penta1-derived, Penta1 population growth, ANC1 population growth (Vaccination denominator chip) (#choose-the-denominator)
Select Best Population: Live births, Total births, Total population or Under 1 year (DHIS2) (#select-best-population)

Denominator Selection: read the survey comparison (National Coverage), the regional pattern (Subnational Derived Coverage), then the trend over time (#denominator-selection)
Set the denominator selector(s) and record why in your notes (#choose-the-denominator)

Missing survey coverage values in Load Data leave the survey comparison empty (#common-pitfalls)
Vaxx: one vaccination denominator, no separate maternal one (#choose-the-denominator)
The method, and how to read these charts, is in Denominator assessment and selection (/en/docs/methodology/denominators/)

sections.heading: Exports, reports and AI
sections.text: This page covers what you can take out of the app (images, tables, datasets and reports), how to build a report, and how the DataSuite chat assistant can analyse the same saved dataset. For planning what to do with the results, see Dissemination, decisions and action and Leveraging AI for analysis and interpretation.

Some charts also offer tools in the card toolbar: edit the labels of one chart, change orientation, text size or legend position, adjust style (fonts, colours, gridlines) and expand the chart. Customize this chart lets you apply a setting to this chart, to every chart of the card, to every chart of the same type or to all charts, and to the screen, the report or both. Settings are saved with the dataset.

[Vaxx] Every chart has a toolbar in its card header:

How to share a chart so readers can check it: Dissemination > Sharing charts and tables.

The wizard also saves the whole analysis as name_vaccine.rds (see Getting started). That file is the cache used by the AI tools below and by the Pooled App.

sections.heading: Reports
sections.text: The Reports page in the Output section builds documents (Word or PDF) and slide decks (PowerPoint or PDF) from the loaded dataset, starting from the standard reports of this app or from a blank page. In the Vaxx app it needs adjusted data. Charts and tables are redrawn from the data every time, and every report is saved in the dataset. The full guide, with each standard report, the editor, export formats and troubleshooting, is on the Reports page.

sections.heading: The DataSuite chat assistant
sections.text: The DataSuite chat assistant works on the same saved dataset as the app, knows which page you are on, and answers from your data and the Countdown methodology, with its sources. What it can and cannot do, and good practice, are on the AI assistant page.

sections.heading: Save your work
sections.text:
[RMNCAH] Finish loading the dataset. The assistant works on the saved _rmncah.rds dataset, which is created when you finish the Load Data wizard.

[Vaxx] Finish the wizard so that the dataset is saved as an .rds cache, and adjust the data.

sections.heading: Ask a question
sections.text:
Open the chat and ask.

[RMNCAH] Examples: List the pages of the RMNCAH app and what each one reads, Which regions have Penta3 coverage below 80% in the latest year, using the selected denominator?, Draft an interpretation of the national continuum of care for the review meeting.

[Vaxx] For example: "Which districts have Penta1 to Penta3 dropout above 10 percent in the latest year?" or "Explain why the survey and DHIS2 Measles 1 coverage differ."

sections.heading: Check the answer
sections.text: The assistant ends its answer with its sources: the data it used and the methodology sections. Compare its numbers with the matching page and charts in the app before quoting them, and see the AI chapter for good prompts.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
- Sharing results: see Dissemination > Common pitfalls.
- Asking the assistant about results before Data Adjustment has been run and saved in the app.
- Accepting an AI interpretation without checking data quality. The assistant reads the same data, so poor data give poor conclusions. AI output must be checked by an analyst. See Leveraging AI for analysis and interpretation.

sections.heading: Limits
sections.text:
- In the Vaxx app, the data reference lists the 18 Vaxx analysis pages (upload, data quality, preparation, denominators, coverage, inequality, equity and targets). It does not describe the Introduction and Reports pages.
- In the Vaxx app, Ask AI buttons in the chart toolbars are not active yet. Use the chat assistant instead.
