sections.heading: Analysis setup
sections.text:
This page describes the steps required to set up the analysis workbench. It sets out the data and national parameters the analysis needs, and how to load them in the apps.

At a glance

- Answers: What data, reference datasets and national parameters does the analysis need, and how are they loaded?
- Uses: the Excel workbook generated from HMIS/DHIS2 exports (see the DHIS2 data indicator definitions), the embedded reference datasets and the national survey parameters.
- Produces: a working folder with the companion .rds file, the reference datasets matched to the country, and the national parameters used for denominator selection; the next step is data quality assessment.
- In the apps: Getting started (the Load Data wizard).

sections.heading: HMIS data
sections.text:
The app accepts common tabular data formats for the DHIS2 upload:

- Excel workbook: .xlsx or .xls
- Stata dataset: .dta
- A dataset already saved by the app: .rds

The Excel workbook, in the format produced by the Data Extractor, must contain an Admin_data sheet, a Population_data sheet, a Reporting_completeness sheet and at least one Service_data sheet.

See the DHIS2 data indicator definitions.

sections.heading: Checks on the uploaded data
Survey files and shapefile
sections.text:
Survey data files (.dta) are optional. There are five: national, regional, area, maternal education and wealth index quintile data. They power equity analysis (the Equity Assessment), survey comparison lines and sub-national comparisons. Without them the app keeps its built-in reference data.

A shapefile is used for maps. A standard shapefile for the country is built in; a custom one can be used instead.

When survey files or a custom shapefile name their regions differently from the dataset, their region (admin-1) names must be matched to those in the dataset.

sections.heading: Embedded datasets
sections.text:
In addition to the uploaded DHIS2 dataset, the app includes internal reference datasets that are linked to the country whose data was uploaded.

These embedded datasets are:

- UN estimates
- Survey data
- WUENIC estimates
- UN mortality data
- Family Planning Estimation Tool (FPET) data

Because these datasets are named according to the country whose DHIS2 data is loaded, the app can automatically match the uploaded file to the correct reference set.

Best practice

- Use one working folder per country or DHIS2 export batch.
- Keep the original Excel source file and the generated .rds file together.
- Do not rename the .rds file manually; the app manages that file automatically.

sections.heading: National parameters for denominator calculation
sections.text:
- These parameters are used to support selection of denominators for service coverage analysis within the RMNCAH analytical framework.
- They are typically derived from the most recent national survey (e.g., DHS, MICS) and are applied uniformly across subnational units.

Tip

The default values are extracted from the available country survey data. Users can update these values if they have more recent, validated values.

Every parameter is required. Coverage values are percentages (0 to 100). Pregnancy loss, twin births, stillbirth, neonatal mortality and post-neonatal mortality are proportions (0 to 0.05; for example 0.03 means 3%). The recent survey year lies between 2015 and 2030.

Analysis parameters

Parameter | Definition
ANC1 Survey (%) | Percentage of women aged 15–49 with a live birth who received at least one antenatal care (ANC) visit during their last pregnancy. (Example: If 940 out of 1,000 women had at least one ANC visit, the ANC1 coverage is 94%.)
ANC4 | Percentage of women aged 15–49 with a live birth who received four or more antenatal care visits during their last pregnancy. (Example: If 680 out of 1,000 women had ≥4 ANC visits, ANC4 coverage is 68%.)
Pregnancy Loss (proportion) | Proportion of pregnancies that ended in miscarriage, abortion, or stillbirth out of all reported pregnancy outcomes. (Example: If 80 of 1,000 pregnancies ended in loss, the proportion is 0.08)
Twin Births (proportion) | Proportion of live births that are twins out of all live births. (Example: If 30 out of 1,500 live births were twins (i.e., 15 twin pairs), the proportion is 0.02)
Neonatal Mortality (proportion) | Proportion of live births that die within the first 28 days of life out of all live births. (Example: If 20 out of 1,000 live births died within the first 28 days, the proportion is 0.02)
Post Neonatal Mortality (proportion) | Proportion of live births that die between 28 days and 11 months of life out of all live births. (Example: If 15 out of 1,000 live births died between 28 days and 11 months, the proportion is 0.015)
Stillbirth Rate (proportion) | Proportion of pregnancies that ended in stillbirth out of all reported pregnancy outcomes. (Example: If 10 out of 1,000 pregnancies ended in stillbirth, the proportion is 0.01)
Institutional delivery | Percentage of live births that occurred in a health facility. (Example: If 850 out of 1,000 live births were in a health facility, the institutional delivery coverage is 85%.)
BCG Coverage (%) | Percentage of infants aged 12–23 months who received the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine. (Example: If 950 out of 1,000 infants received the BCG vaccine, the BCG coverage is 95%.)
Penta1 Coverage (%) | Percentage of infants aged 12–23 months who received the first dose of pentavalent vaccine. (Example: If 920 out of 1,000 infants received the first dose, the Penta 1 coverage is 92%.)
Penta 3 | Percentage of infants aged 12–23 months who received the third dose of pentavalent vaccine. (Example: If 850 out of 1,000 infants received the third dose, the Penta 3 coverage is 85%.)
Measles 1 Coverage (%) | Percentage of infants aged 12–23 months who received the first dose of measles vaccine. (Example: If 900 out of 1,000 infants received the first dose, the Measles1 coverage is 90%.)
C-Section Rate (%) | Percentage of live births that were delivered by cesarean section. (Example: If 150 out of 1,000 live births were by C-section, the C-section coverage is 15%.)
Low birth weight | Percentage of live births that were low birth weight (less than 2,500 grams). (Example: If 100 out of 1,000 live births were low birth weight, the low birth weight coverage is 10%.)
Recent survey Year | The calendar year in which the survey was conducted and from which vaccine coverage estimates (e.g., BCG, Penta1/3, Measles1) are drawn. (Example: If the survey was conducted in 2022, that is the vaccine survey year).
Survey Data Start Year | The calendar year from which the survey data starts. This is used to determine the time period for which the survey data is relevant. Ideally, it is recommended to use the two most recent surveys for this analysis. (Example: If a country has survey data for 2008, 2013, 2018 and 2023; the Survey data start should be 2018 (two most recent)).

RMNCAH and vaccine analyses differ here: ANC4, C-section rate and low birth weight are asked for in RMNCAH analyses only; vaccine analyses ask instead for the OPV1 and OPV3 survey coverage. See RMNCAH and vaccine analyses.

sections.heading: In the apps
sections.text: Setup is done in the app's Load Data wizard; Getting started describes it screen by screen, including the national parameter fields.

sections.heading: Create a working folder
sections.text:
The first step in the analysis workflow is to prepare a dedicated working folder. This folder is where you keep the input files for the app, and where the system creates the derived data file used for faster future loads.

- Choose a clear directory name that you can easily remember and reference, preferably in your local environment.
- Place the raw upload (Excel) files in that folder before starting the app.
- Keep any related documentation, data or country-specific files together so the working folder is self-contained.

sections.heading: Uploading HMIS data
sections.text: For the initial upload, use the Excel workbook generated from HMIS/DHIS2 exports. For subsequent uploads, use the cached .RDS file, which is automatically generated and stored in the working folder when the Excel file is uploaded.

sections.heading: Automatic RDS creation
sections.text:
- When you load an Excel file for the first time, the app automatically converts and saves a companion .rds file in the same working folder.
- On subsequent loads, the app checks for the existing .rds file and uses it to speed up data reloads.

This means the first load may take slightly longer while the Excel file is read and transformed. After that, the app opens the saved .rds file much faster.

sections.heading: Bayesian modeling approach
sections.text:
We developed a statistical model to estimate health coverage at the national level and for subnational regions up to the most recent year with data, and to make short-term forecasts for the years ahead.

At a glance

- Answers: What is the best estimate of coverage in each year, nationally and for subnational regions, up to the most recent year with data and for the years just ahead, and how uncertain is it?
- Uses: household survey data (their coverage levels, weighted by their uncertainty) and routine facility data (only their year-to-year trend, from National coverage), with the Countdown mean data quality score from Data quality assessment.
- Produces: for ANC4, institutional deliveries and vaccination coverage (three doses of pentavalent), a best estimate for each year with a 95% uncertainty interval, nationally and by region, and short-term forecasts. Next: Equity assessment (equiplots).
- In the apps: Bayesian Analysis (RMNCAH app only).

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text:
Reliable information on health coverage indicators is essential for monitoring progress, informing programs, and guiding policy decisions.
However, relying on survey and routine data alone is often challenging.
Routine data from facilities may suffer from underreporting or inconsistent data quality, while survey data may be uncertain or not recent.

To address these challenges, statistical models can be used to produce estimates and forecasts over time, combining multiple data sources and accounting for their limitations.
This results in estimates of coverage every year (between data points and past data) with an indication of how certain/uncertain we are about each year.
As a result, models enable more complete, accurate, and timely assessments of health coverage, especially in data-limited settings.

The model is the tool to use when surveys are old or few and facility data are imperfect, and a single defensible trend is needed, for example for a synthesis report.

sections.heading: Producing estimates and short-term forecasts
sections.text:
The model looks at the available data and identifies different ways coverage could have changed over time. Each of these possible paths is called a trajectory (see the figure in the section on how survey data are used).

For each year, we report a best estimate (the middle value across all trajectories) and a range that shows the uncertainty (leaving out the most extreme possibilities at the edge).

Informed by global analyses, the model captures that over time coverage usually rises from low to high levels, following an S-shaped trend, with periods of faster or slower progress along the way depending on what the data indicates. It uses survey and routine data to choose trajectories that match what has been observed. The model also draws on trends seen in other areas with similar coverage levels.

sections.heading: How are survey data used?
sections.text:
Survey data help us understand coverage, but they come with some uncertainty. This happens because surveys only include a sample of the population, not everyone, and there can be errors during data collection.

To best use survey data, the model tries to strike the right balance—smoothing out random ups and downs that are probably not real, while still capturing important patterns in the data. To do this, the model looks at how uncertain each data point is:

- High uncertainty: If a data point is very uncertain, it will have less impact on estimated coverage (the model gives it less weight and is more likely to smooth over it).
- High reliability: If a data point is more reliable, estimates will align closer to that value.

For subnational regions, the model uses survey data from the specific region when available.

Possible coverage trajectories over time based on survey data

sections.heading: How are routine data used?
sections.text:
The coverage estimates from routine data can be biased, so the model treats it differently from survey data. For surveys, the model uses the actual coverage levels. For example, if a survey indicates coverage at 60% for a particular year, the model uses that value directly.

In contrast, routine data can be biased due to issues such as incomplete reporting and data collection inconsistencies. Due to this, the model does not rely on coverage levels observed in routine data. Instead, the model focuses on the trend over time—specifically, how coverage changes from year to year.

- Example: If routine data shows coverage increasing from 50% in 2020 to 53% in 2021, the model interprets this as a 3 percentage point increase. If the routine data shows faster or slower changes than expected, the model adjusts the estimates—but only as much as the data can be trusted.

Accounting for data quality

The model accounts for routine data quality by adjusting the uncertainty of the trend estimates. Observations with lower data quality are treated as more uncertain and given less weight in determining true rates of change. Specifically, uncertainty in the estimated rate of change increases as the Countdown mean data quality score decreases. Consequently, lower-quality data exerts less influence on the modeled rate of change.

sections.text:
Estimates are produced for:

- The proportion of women who receive the recommended minimum of at least four antenatal care visits during pregnancy (ANC4).
- The proportion of live births that take place in a health facility (Institutional deliveries).
- The proportion of children who receive the recommended three doses of pentavalent vaccine (Vaccination coverage).

sections.heading: Example 3: Data and Bayesian estimates
sections.text:
The figure below shows example data and estimates obtained from the model for a coverage indicator in four different regions.

Survey data, routine data, and Bayesian estimates for four regions

Interpretation

- Survey data from DHS and MICS are shown in red and blue, with vertical bars indicating how uncertain each survey point is. Routine data are shown in black. The lines represent the model's point estimates with shaded areas highlighting uncertainty (in red if routine data were included, black/green otherwise).
- The plots show that the model's estimates usually follow the survey data, unless a data point is very uncertain and does not match the overall trend.
- For example, in Region B, the most recent MICS survey point is lower than expected and very uncertain, so the model's recent estimates do not exactly align with this survey.
- We also see that routine data help inform how quickly coverage is changing over time, particularly after the most recent survey, when no new survey data is available.
- Region C: The routine data show an increase in coverage. As a result, the estimates that include routine data show a faster rate of change during that period compared to the estimates based only on survey data.
- Region D: Routine data suggest that coverage has not increased recently, and estimates that include routine data reflect that information.

sections.heading: Reading the estimates
sections.text: A narrow band means the data agree; a wide band means few or conflicting data points. The estimate follows an S-shaped rise typical of coverage. Do not read the model as a replacement for good data: if the routine data quality score is low, the estimate leans on surveys.

sections.heading: National coverage
sections.text:
Once data quality is assured, denominators selected, and numerators adjusted, the DataSuite synthesizes everything into coverage estimates—the core metric that answers: What proportion of the population needing a health service actually received it? This module generates annual coverage estimates for reproductive, maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health indicators by dividing adjusted numerators from facility reports by the best-performing population denominators. Coverage estimates are then compared with recent household survey results to validate findings and identify areas of systematic bias.

At a glance

- Answers: What proportion of the population needing a health service actually received it, year by year at national level, and do surveys (and WUENIC for immunization) confirm the facility-based estimates?
- Uses: adjusted numerators from Data adjustment and the denominators chosen in Denominator assessment and selection; household survey estimates, WUENIC for immunization and FPET for family planning.
- Produces: annual national coverage estimates and trends for each indicator, compared with surveys and targets; maternal/newborn and child continuum-of-care profiles; subnational heatmaps and best/worst performers. Next: Bayesian modeling approach and Subnational analysis.
- In the apps: National Coverage; Continuum of Care and FP Projection (RMNCAH app).
- Defaults: Defaults and thresholds: Coverage

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The scientific and programmatic basis for measuring coverage of antenatal care, delivery care, immunization and family planning is set out in the rationale; each indicator group under Method links to its own section there.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text:
Coverage estimation must account for operational realities: some indicators (institutional deliveries, immunizations) reach implausibly high levels (>100%) due to data quality issues or duplicate recording, requiring reframing as average services per capita rather than percentages. Family planning coverage is handled through specialized demographic modeling (FPET) that integrates multiple survey data sources and can incorporate facility data if quality permits. The module produces trend lines, comparisons with global targets (e.g., 90% institutional delivery by 2025), and side-by-side facility-versus-survey visualizations for credibility assessment.

RMNCAH and vaccine analyses differ here: RMNCAH analyses estimate coverage for ANC, delivery (including C-section and low birth weight), postnatal care, a small set of vaccines and family planning (FPET projection), and add the maternal and child continuum of care; vaccine analyses estimate coverage for ANC1, institutional deliveries and live births and the routine vaccines (BCG, IPV, measles, OPV, Penta, PCV, rotavirus), with dropout, zero-dose and under-vaccinated children. See RMNCAH and vaccine analyses.

sections.heading: Antenatal care (ANC)
sections.text:
See the rationale: Antenatal care (ANC).

Most countries have at least one ANC indicator with a target in the national plan. The global ENAP/EPMM coverage targets for 2025 are: globally, at least 90% of pregnant women with 4 or more ANC care visits, and 90% of countries with at least 70% coverage. There are several ANC indicators that capture:

- Contact with health services during pregnancy (ANC 1st visit, ANC 4 or more visits, ANC first visit in first trimester). ANC1 is often considered an indicator of basic access to health services. It is high in most countries, and in many instances, the numbers of ANC1 visits in the routine health facility data can provide a better denominator for the ANC and delivery indicators than population projections (see section 2 on denominators).
- Contents of services provided (intermittent preventive therapy (IPT2 or IPT3) against malaria, HIV testing, syphilis testing and iron-folic acid (IFA) supplementation (at least 90 tablets given to the pregnant woman)). Some countries will not have policies for all of these diagnostic or therapeutic interventions during pregnancy (e.g., no IPT if no malaria risk).

For most indicators, the surveys also provide coverage estimates for the national level, with 95% confidence intervals. For most coverage indicators the data refer to a period before the survey: e.g., institutional birth coverage for the live births in the two years preceding the survey. This means that the midpoint of the coverage estimate lies one year before the survey.

Sometimes, an indicator may reach an unlikely high coverage at the national level, say over 125%. This may be because the data quality of the numerator of the coverage indicator is poor, the denominator is wrong, or the intervention is given and recorded more than once during pregnancy. An example is IFA supplementation. In that case, the computation of coverage is not useful. It is better to express it differently. For instance, if coverage is 200%, it is better to compute the average number of courses of 90 IFA tablets that a pregnant woman received (in this case 2.0 per pregnant woman in the population).

National ANC4 coverage, facility and survey estimates

sections.heading: Delivery care
sections.text:
See the rationale: Delivery care.

All countries have at least one delivery care indicator with a target in the national plan. The global Every Newborn Action Plan (ENAP) and Ending Preventable Maternal Mortality (EPMM) coverage target for 2025 is at least 90% global average coverage, and 90% of countries with at least 80% coverage of skilled birth attendance (SBA). For postnatal care (PNC) within 2 days, the global coverage target is 80%, and 90% of countries with at least 60% coverage.

Institutional (live) birth coverage and SBA are closely related, as almost all deliveries with a skilled attendant occur in health facilities. From the analytical perspective, institutional birth coverage is preferred because it is a more objective measure and avoids issues with varying national definitions of what constitutes a skilled birth. SBA is often preferred from the healthcare perspective because it includes an element of quality; obviously, an institutional delivery without skilled attendance is not desirable, and in some countries, home SBA may be part of the healthcare delivery strategy. Either indicator works well to capture delivery care.

Caesarean section is a life-saving intervention and an important indicator. A general rule of thumb put forward by the World Health Organization (WHO) is that the population-level need for Caesarean section is in the range of 10–15% of all deliveries.

- Below 10%: Indicates an unmet need for surgical delivery care.
- Over 10–15%: Implies a likely overuse of Caesarean section. It may also imply a combination of unmet need among certain population groups (e.g., the poorest or rural women) alongside overuse in other subgroups (such as urban and wealthier women).

Postnatal care (PNC) within 48 hours is provided to the mother and newborn. Country systems vary in how they record the type of PNC, and household surveys are known to have data quality issues regarding PNC for the mother or the baby. Some countries use multiple definitions for the timing of the PNC visit (e.g., within the first week).

Low birthweight is a critical indicator of neonatal health. It is most meaningful if the distinction between prematurity and small-for-gestational-age is made, but most facility reporting systems and surveys lack such granular data. All babies are supposed to be weighed immediately after birth, and the percentage of newborns weighing less than 2,500 grams is typically reported in the DHIS2 system. As general guidance for data interpretation, low birthweight prevalence in sub-Saharan Africa was estimated at 13.9% (95% credibility interval: 12.4–15.7%) for 2020.

National low birth weight coverage

sections.heading: Immunization
sections.text:
See the rationale: Immunization.

Immunization coverage indicators are included in virtually every country's health sector monitoring plan. A general target is at least 90% coverage for essential vaccines given in childhood and adolescence.

For national coverage analyses, the focus is on BCG, the first and third doses of pentavalent/DTP (penta1/DTP1 and penta3/DTP3), and the first and second doses of the measles vaccine (often co-administered as measles-rubella). BCG and penta/DTP vaccinations are recommended at birth (BCG), 6 weeks (penta1), and 14 weeks (penta3).

- Facility data: The number of vaccinations given to infants is used as the numerator. The denominator is the number of eligible children in the population, approximated as:
  $\text{Denominator} = \text{Live Births} - \text{Neonatal Deaths}$
- Survey data: Generally provide vaccination coverage among children aged 12–23 months (and may include the age at which the vaccination was administered, typically before the first birthday).

The first dose of measles vaccine is generally recommended at age 9 months. For facility data, recording and reporting usually separate measles doses given to children under 1 year from those given to children 1 year and older, though recording quality by age group varies (there is often a tendency to record measles vaccinations administered after 12 months as given to infants). Here, the denominator used to measure coverage represents children who survived the first year of life:
$\text{Measles 1 Denominator} = \text{Live Births} - \text{Neonatal Deaths} - \text{Postneonatal Deaths}$

The second dose of measles uses children aged 24–35 months as the denominator, estimated as:
$\text{Measles 2 Denominator} = \text{Live Births} - \text{Neonatal Deaths} - (2 \times \text{Postneonatal Deaths})$

Vaccine analyses also compute dropout (Penta 1 to Penta 3, Penta 1 to Measles 1, Penta 3 to Measles 1, Measles 1 to Measles 2) and zero-dose and under-vaccinated children. Dropout is the number of children who received the first dose minus those who received the second, divided by the first, as a percentage. Zero-dose and under-vaccinated are derived from Penta1 and Penta3.

WHO and UNICEF collaborate with countries to produce annual estimates of immunization coverage using all data sources. These national estimates, called WUENIC, are published and available for 2020–2024. These time trends are included in the analysis outputs to compare the 2019–2024 annual facility data estimates produced in the workshop against the survey results.

National measles first dose coverage

sections.heading: Family planning
sections.text:
See the rationale: Family planning.

Family planning coverage estimates are derived from a collaboration between Countdown to 2030 and Track20. Track20 developed the Family Planning Estimation Tool (FPET), an advanced model focusing on three indicators: modern contraceptive use, unmet need for modern contraceptives, and demand satisfied with modern methods. These three indicators are closely related because:

$\text{Demand Satisfied (Coverage)} = \frac{\text{Use of Modern Contraceptives}}{\text{Unmet Need} + \text{Use of Modern Contraceptives}}$

FPET uses statistical modeling that incorporates all available survey data and can integrate facility data if the quality is sufficient. FPET allows various types of survey data to be combined, fitting a trend line that draws strength from multiple data points and minimizes the risks associated with directly comparing different surveys.

In the apps, the FPET estimates are built-in reference data for the country; they do not come from your facility data.

FPET projections

sections.heading: National coverage trends
sections.text:
- The national trend graph shows annual facility-based coverage, usually from 2020–2025 or the latest available period.
- Survey estimates are overlaid using at least last two household surveys, with confidence intervals where available.
- For immunization indicators, WUENIC estimates may also be shown as an external reference.
- Is facility-based coverage increasing, declining, or stagnating?
  
  - Are the last two survey estimates consistent with the facility trend?
  - For immunization, do facility data, survey data, and WUENIC tell a similar story?
  - Is the country moving toward the relevant national or global target?

National penta3 coverage

National measles1 coverage

National ANC4 coverage

sections.heading: Interpreting the national trend
sections.text:
- If facility and survey estimates are close, confidence in the trend is stronger: DHIS2 lines that track the survey and WUENIC points support the chosen denominator.
- If facility estimates are much higher than survey estimates, check for denominator issues, over-reporting, or incomplete private-sector adjustment.
- If facility estimates are much lower than survey estimates, check for incomplete facility reporting, missing outreach services, missing private-sector data, or extraction problems.
- A persistent gap points to a denominator or numerator problem; go back to Data quality and Denominators.
- Wide survey confidence intervals mean the survey point should be interpreted cautiously. Survey points are few and have confidence intervals: do not over-read small differences.
- Coverage above 100% should be treated as a data-quality signal, not as strong program performance.

sections.heading: Maternal and newborn continuum of care
sections.text:
- The maternal/newborn continuum graph follows the pathway from pregnancy to delivery and the immediate postnatal period.
- Typical indicators include:
  
  - First-trimester ANC
  - ANC4+
  - Institutional live births
  - Postnatal care within 48 hours

Maternal and newborn continuum of care

sections.heading: Interpreting the maternal continuum
sections.text:
- The graph helps identify where women and newborns are being lost along the care pathway.
- Low first-trimester ANC suggests delayed entry into pregnancy care.
- Gap between first-trimester ANC and ANC4+ suggests weak continuity of antenatal care.
- High ANC but lower institutional live births may indicate barriers to delivery care, such as distance, transport, cost, referral gaps, or perceived quality of care.
- High institutional live births but low postnatal care suggests missed opportunities before discharge or weak follow-up after birth.
- If facility and survey estimates are consistent, the interpretation is stronger.
- If facility and survey estimates differ, check indicator definitions, reporting completeness, denominator quality, private-sector reporting, and survey timing.

sections.heading: Child continuum of care
sections.text:
- The child continuum graph focuses on child health contacts after birth, especially immunization and child illness services.
- Current priority indicators may include:
  
  - DTP3/Penta3
  - MCV1/Measles1
  - BCG, DTP1, MCV2, PCV3, rotavirus, full immunization, zero-dose, ORS, and pneumonia care-seeking where available.
- The graph helps assess whether children remain in contact with services after birth and access to essential immunization services.

Child continuum of care

sections.heading: Interpreting the child continuum
sections.text:
- A gap between DTP3/Penta3 and MCV1 may suggest dropout after the early infant vaccine series.
- Low MCV1 compared with DTP3 may point to weak follow-up, missed opportunities, caregiver mobility, or reporting gaps.
- For immunization indicators, compare facility data, survey estimates, and WUENIC.
- If all three sources align, confidence in the immunization coverage pattern is stronger.
- If facility data are higher than both survey and WUENIC, check denominators, reported doses, and possible over-reporting.
- If facility data are lower than survey or WUENIC, check completeness of reporting, outreach data capture, private-sector reporting, and extraction issues.

sections.heading: Subnational heatmaps
sections.text:
- Heatmaps show variation across subnational units.
- The color scale should be read as:
  
  - Red = lower coverage / weaker performance.
  - Yellow/orange = intermediate coverage.
  - Green = higher coverage / stronger performance.
- Read the heatmap across rows to understand how one subnational area performs across multiple indicators.
- Read the heatmap down columns to understand how one indicator varies across subnational areas.

Maternal continuum heatmap by admin 1 area

Child continuum heatmap by admin 1 area

sections.heading: Continuum of care at subnational level
sections.text:
- A row with many red cells suggests broad service delivery, access, or reporting challenges in that area.
- A column with many red cells suggests that the indicator is a national bottleneck.
- A mixed row suggests that the area performs well for some services but poorly for others.
- Green areas may provide useful lessons, but they should still be checked for data quality.
- Red areas should trigger deeper review, but low values may reflect reporting or denominator problems rather than true low coverage, so check quality before acting.

sections.heading: Best and worst subnational performance
sections.text:
- Best and worst areas should not be classified using latest coverage alone.
- Interpretation should consider:
  
  - Latest coverage level.
  - Change over time.
  - Reporting completeness.
  - Denominator quality.
  - Implausible values above 100%.
- A useful classification is:
  
  - High and improving – strong performance; potential learning area.
  - High but declining – early warning area.
  - Low but improving – progress area needing continued support.
  - Low and declining – priority area for review and corrective action.
- Areas with coverage above 100% should be flagged and excluded from best performance rankings unless data are reviewed.
- Countries should examine whether poor performance is concentrated in a few areas or widespread across many areas.

Best and worst admin 1 areas by indicator

sections.heading: Family planning projections
sections.text:
- Lines are median estimates and shaded bands are 95% credible intervals.

FPET fits a trend through all available surveys, so a smooth curve does not mean a survey exists for each year.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
- Zero-dose and under-vaccinated children (vaccine analyses) depend on the denominator even more than dose coverage does.
- Reading the FP Projection as a facility indicator. It is model output.
- Interpreting the continuum heatmap without first checking Data quality for the region.

sections.heading: Data adjustment
sections.text:
Missing reports and data errors distort coverage analysis, particularly when reporting rates are low or sporadic. This module applies evidence-based corrections to transform raw reported numbers into defensible estimates by accounting for non-reporting facilities and removing extreme outliers.
Using a scientifically grounded adjustment factor—based on assumptions about relative service volumes in reporting versus non-reporting facilities—DataSuite scales up numbers proportionally to reflect the true population-level coverage.

At a glance

- Answers: How should the reported numbers be corrected for incomplete reporting, extreme outliers and missing values, so that coverage is not underestimated?
- Uses: the reporting completeness, extreme outliers and missing values assessed in Data quality assessment, and the adjustment factor $k$ set by the analyst.
- Produces: the adjusted numbers ($N_{\text{adj}}$), a master adjusted dataset (.dta), used as the numerators of the coverage statistics in Denominator assessment and selection and Coverage.
- In the apps: Data preparation (Remove Years, Data Adjustment and Data Adjustment Changes).
- Defaults: Defaults and thresholds: data adjustment

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The adjustment strategy is pragmatic: if we assume all non-reporting facilities provided zero services, we dramatically underestimate true coverage. Instead, the module estimates what proportion of services likely occurred in silent facilities (a share k of the reporting facilities' volume, set by the analyst; the Countdown guidebook's default is 25%) and adjusts accordingly. Where a district's reporting for a month is critically low (below 75%) or missing, its reporting rate is replaced by the district's median rate from its months at 75–100% before adjusting, so a few very incomplete months cannot produce impossible estimates (see Critical data threshold rules).

sections.heading: Rationale: scientific basis for the analysis
sections.text:
The completeness of institutional reporting can heavily distort coverage analysis, particularly if reporting levels are low or fluctuate significantly between years.

Similarly, extreme outliers—such as an accidental extra zero keyed during data entry—can exert a disproportionate impact, especially on sub-national metrics. Following our baseline data quality assessments, corrective steps are necessary to generate a clean, standardized dataset for final analysis. This requires mathematically adjusting for incomplete reporting and resolving extreme outliers.

For the longer argument, see Reporting completeness: rationale and Extreme outliers: rationale.

sections.heading: Approach: description of analytical steps
sections.text:
If we fail to adjust for reporting completeness, we implicitly assume that all non-reporting facilities provided zero health services during their silent periods, which is statistically improbable.

Adjustments depend on estimating the true volume of services (e.g., antenatal care, vaccinations) provided at non-reporting facilities relative to those that submitted data. To do this, we establish an adjustment factor, denoted as $k$.

The adjustment factor $k$ is defined as the ratio of the volume of services provided by non-reporting facilities to the volume of services provided by reporting facilities. This factor is used directly to scale up reported numbers to offset incomplete reporting gaps.

sections.heading: Numerator adjustment formulas and parameters
sections.text:
To accurately account for incomplete reporting, the raw reported number of events is adjusted using both the reporting completeness proportion and the facility service volume ratio via the following equation:

$N_{\text{adj}} = N_{\text{rep}} + N_{\text{rep}} \times \left( \frac{1}{C} - 1 \right) \times k$

Where:

- $N_{\text{adj}}$: Total estimated number of health events adjusted for incomplete reporting.
- $N_{\text{rep}}$: Raw number of events reported in the system.
- $C$: Reporting completeness (expressed as the proportion of expected facility reports actually received).
- $k$: The adjustment factor accounting for lower relative service volumes in non-reporting facilities.

sections.heading: Configuring the k-factor
sections.text:
A new dataset starts at k = 0 (no adjustment) until the analyst sets k for each service on the Data Adjustment page. The Countdown guidebook's default is k = 0.25, which assumes that non-reporting facilities are active but operate at a lower capacity, providing a service volume equivalent to exactly one-quarter (25%) of an average reporting facility.

However, the factor $k$ can be adjusted manually for different services based on system context. For example, if private health facilities have poor reporting compliance but handle a large share of maternal deliveries nationally, $k$ may be raised above 0.25, or set as high as 1.0. More generally, raise a factor when facilities that report poorly, such as private ones, provide a large share of that service; keep the guidebook's default of 0.25 unless you have evidence that non-reporting facilities carry a different share of services.

Depending on local infrastructure, you can select from the following k-value tiers:

- k = 0.00 – No services provided in non-reporting facilities.
- k = 0.25 – Some services provided, but at a volume much lower than reporting facilities (the guidebook's default).
- k = 0.50 – Services provided at half the rate compared to reporting facilities.
- k = 0.75 – Services provided at nearly the same rate as reporting facilities.
- k = 1.00 – Services provided at the exact same rate as reporting facilities.

RMNCAH and vaccine analyses differ here: k is set per service: four k-factors in RMNCAH analyses (ANC, Delivery, Vaccines and OPD), three in vaccine analyses (ANC, Delivery and Vaccines); see Choose the K-Factors. See RMNCAH and vaccine analyses.

sections.heading: Critical data threshold rules
sections.text:
- The 75% completeness rule: If a district's reporting rate for a service is below 75% in a month (or missing), that rate is not used as it is: it is replaced by the median of the district's reporting rates between 75% and 100% for that service. The month's reported count is then adjusted with the adjustment factor $k$ as usual -- no month is left unadjusted, and the reported count itself is kept. (The 2024 Countdown vaccination guidebook words this both as "no adjustment below 75%" and as "median value imputed"; the rule above is the one the apps apply.)
- Outlier correction: A monthly value more than 5 times the MAD from the district's median monthly value (median and MAD computed from all years except the most recent one) is an extreme outlier; it is replaced by the median of the district's other (non-outlier) months in the same year.

sections.heading: Summary of data adjustment business rules
sections.text:

below 75%

median of the district's reporting rates between 75% and 100%

for that service; the month's reported count is then adjusted with

$k$

between $\ge$ 75% and $\le$ 100%

In RMNCAH analyses, mortality indicators are not adjusted for reporting or outliers, because deaths are few and volatile (see Mortality).

sections.heading: Remove years
sections.text:
The Remove Years configuration panel allows you to completely exclude specific calendar years from the active processing pipeline. This tool is designed to drop years that contain zero reporting data, or whose data has been explicitly flagged as unfit for analysis by the national technical team due to severe, systemic quality issues.

Remove a year only when the data quality checks show that it is clearly erratic or unusable -- for example a year with almost no reporting or a known, system-wide failure -- and you have a real-world reason to believe it. If you have no reason, keep the year.

It is highly recommended to use this feature when:

- The quantitative data quality baseline falls well below acceptable standard thresholds.
- The country team possesses sufficient, verified contextual information (e.g., major system-wide roll-out failures, prolonged network blackouts, or database corruption events) that render that specific year's data completely unreliable or inaccurate.

Strategically removing these corrupted historical blocks ensures that your subsequent coverage timelines and trend assessments are built exclusively upon a robust, reliable data foundation.

sections.heading: Adjustment outputs
sections.text:
This section produces a master adjusted dataset (.dta) ready for analysis, along with plots for different indicators showing the effect of data adjustments. The image below shows the adjustment output after making no adjustment to the data.

Data adjustment screen with k-factor selection

Data adjustment changes comparing values before and after adjustment

Reading the before-and-after comparison:

- A small gap between the lines (small differences between before and after) is normal and means reporting was already nearly complete.
- A wide gap or large jump in one year points to a year with very low reporting, or to an outlier that needs a second look in Outlier Detection. Report the k-factor used and the percentage change it produced (see Report).
- The effect is largest for services with the lowest reporting rates. Compare with the Reporting Rate page.

sections.heading: Report
sections.text:
The interpretation should include the selected adjustment factor (factor k) that was used to adjust for incomplete reporting (if necessary, by service). If the default factor is used, then report this and explain what this means for the reader.

Report the percentage change the adjustment produced in reported numbers of institutional deliveries and penta1 over the six-year period.

You may wish to:

- Highlight the year with the greatest impact of the adjustment if there is one.
- Interpret if the impact of the adjustment on coverage rates is large or small.
- Make the same description and interpretations for penta1 vaccinations.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
- Removing a year you should keep silently shortens every later trend.
- Using a high k-factor to hide poor reporting hides the problem instead of fixing it. Document your choice.
- Months or districts with reporting below 75 percent are not left unadjusted (see Critical data threshold rules), but adjustment cannot recover what very incomplete reporting missed, so consider removing such years.

sections.heading: Remove unreliable years
sections.text:
On the Remove Years page, select the years to exclude and confirm (see Remove Years).

Remove years screen for excluding unreliable years

sections.heading: Choose the k-factor and adjust the data
sections.text:
The outputs and configurations for this phase are managed directly through the Data Adjustment section of the DataSuite.

Within this module's user interface, select the specific $k$-factor value that is deemed appropriate given your unique country context and facility ecosystem in order to execute the data cleaning pipeline (see Data Adjustment).

sections.heading: Review the changes
sections.text: Compare the values before and after adjustment on the Data Adjustment Changes page.

ai.summary: Adjusts facility numbers for incomplete reporting and extreme outliers so coverage is not underestimated. Non- reporting facilities are assumed to provide a fraction k of the service volume of reporting facilities, rather than zero.
definitions: k: the ratio of the volume of services provided by non-reporting facilities to that of reporting facilities (#approach-description-of-analytical-steps)

N_adj = N_rep + N_rep x (1/C - 1) x k, where N_rep is the raw reported number and C the reporting completeness (proportion of expected reports received) (#numerator-adjustment-formulas-and-parameters)
options: k = 0.00: no services in non-reporting facilities (#configuring-the-k-factor)
k = 0.25: some services, at a much lower volume (the guidebook's default) (#configuring-the-k-factor)
k = 0.50: half the rate of reporting facilities (#configuring-the-k-factor)
k = 0.75: nearly the same rate (#configuring-the-k-factor)
k = 1.00: the same rate (#configuring-the-k-factor)
steps: Select the k value appropriate to the country context in the Data Adjustment section, then run the cleaning pipeline (#implementation-conducting-analysis-in-the-datasuite)
rules: A new dataset starts at k = 0 (no adjustment); k is set per service; the guidebook's default is 0.25 unless there is evidence of a different share; raise k (up to 1.0) where poorly reporting facilities (e.g. private) provide a large share of the service (#configuring-the-k-factor)

Reporting below 75% (or missing): the rate is replaced by the median of the district's rates between 75% and 100% for that service; the count is then adjusted with k, not replaced (#critical-data-threshold-rules)
Reporting between 75% and 100%: k scales up the raw numbers (#summary-of-data-adjustment-business-rules)

Extreme outliers (over 5 x MAD from the district's median monthly value, computed without the most recent year) are replaced with the median of the district's non-outlier months that year (#summary-of-data-adjustment-business-rules)
Missing values are imputed with the district median monthly value for that year (#summary-of-data-adjustment-business-rules)
RMNCAH: mortality indicators are not adjusted (deaths are few and volatile) (#summary-of-data-adjustment-business-rules)
Remove Years drops years with zero reporting or flagged unfit by the national technical team (e.g. system-wide failures); with no real-world reason, keep the year (#remove-years)

Report the k used (by service if relevant) and, if the default, what it means; report the percentage change the adjustment produced in institutional deliveries and Penta1 over the period (#report)
Optionally highlight the year with the greatest impact and whether the impact on coverage is large or small (#report)
Removing a year that should be kept shortens every later trend; a high k hides poor reporting instead of fixing it; adjustment cannot recover very incomplete reporting (#common-pitfalls)

sections.heading: Data quality assessment
sections.text:
This module systematically evaluates health facility data by considering the standard data quality metrics, which include:

- Reporting completeness
- Outlier detection
- Internal consistency
- Data missingness
- Ratio calculations
- Overall quality score

At a glance

- Answers: How complete, plausible and internally consistent are the health facility data, before coverage is estimated?
- Uses: the monthly health facility data (reports received and service numbers) and, for the expected ratios, the ANC1, Penta1 and Penta3 (and OPV1, OPV3) coverage from the most recent survey.
- Produces: the metrics 1a-1c, 2a-2b and 3a-3h and the overall quality score; missing values and extreme outliers are then corrected, and unreliable years can be removed, in Data adjustment.
- In the apps: Data quality (Data quality in the RMNCAH app, Data Quality Assessment in the Vaxx app).
- Defaults: Defaults and thresholds: data quality

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text:
High-quality health facility data form the foundation of reliable coverage estimates.
For the scientific basis of each metric, see Data quality assessment: rationale.

sections.heading: Reporting completeness
sections.text:
For further reading on the scientific basis and methods used to assess reporting completeness, go to Reporting completeness: rationale.

Metric | Numerator | Denominator | Interpretation
1a | Number of monthly facility reports received | Total expected reports

(12 × number of facilities) | ≥90% is good; affects trend interpretation
1b | Districts with ≥90% reporting completeness | Total districts | Identifies low-performing districts
1c | Districts with no missing values across all forms | Total districts | Identifies the distribution of missing values across districts

RMNCAH and vaccine analyses differ here: statistics for 1a and 1b are the mean over the analysis's reporting forms: RMNCAH analyses use ANC, delivery, immunization and OPD (inpatient excluded); vaccine analyses use ANC, delivery and immunization. The 2024 Countdown vaccination guidebook based them on the immunization form only. See RMNCAH and vaccine analyses.

sections.heading: Outlier detection
sections.text:
An extreme outlier is defined as a monthly value more than 5 times the median absolute deviation (MAD) away from the median monthly value of the same series (Hampel method) -- the district's, or the national or admin-1 series being assessed. The median and MAD are computed from all years except the most recent one, so the latest year is judged against the earlier years.
For further reading on the scientific basis and methods used to assess and adjust for extreme outliers, go to Extreme outliers: rationale.

Metric | Numerator | Denominator | Interpretation
2a | Monthly values not classified as outliers | Total monthly values | ≥99% expected
2b | Districts with no outliers | Total districts | ≥90% expected

sections.heading: Internal consistency
sections.text:
- Internal consistency assesses the degree to which related indicators are aligned within the dataset, based on expected epidemiological and service delivery relationships.
- Within the CD2030 analytical framework, this step complements other DQA metrics by evaluating whether indicators that are biologically or programmatically linked follow plausible patterns.
- Unlike standalone indicator checks, internal consistency focuses on relationships between indicators, ensuring that reported values reflect realistic service delivery pathways across the continuum of care.

The following metrics are considered when assessing internal consistency:

National ratios:

Metric | Numerator | Denominator | Interpretation
3a | ANC1 reported (national) | Penta1 reported | Expected ratio 1.07 × (ANC1 ÷ Penta1 survey coverage), ± 0.05 (see

Ratio calculations

)
3b | Penta1 reported (national) | Penta3 reported | Expected ratio Penta1 ÷ Penta3 survey coverage, ± 0.05
3c

(vaccine analyses) | OPV1 reported (national) | OPV3 reported | Expected ratio OPV1 ÷ OPV3 survey coverage, ± 0.05

District ratios: the share of districts whose ratio is between 1.0 and 1.5 (a wider range, as district ratios vary more):

Ratio | RMNCAH analyses | Vaccine analyses | Numerator | Denominator
ANC1 / Penta1 | 3c | 3f | Districts with the ratio between 1.0 and 1.5 | Total districts
Penta1 / Penta3 | 3d | 3g | Districts with the ratio between 1.0 and 1.5 | Total districts
OPV1 / OPV3 | – | 3h | Districts with the ratio between 1.0 and 1.5 | Total districts

RMNCAH and vaccine analyses differ here: vaccine analyses add the OPV1/OPV3 ratio (3c nationally, 3h for districts), so the district checks are 3c and 3d in RMNCAH analyses and 3f, 3g and 3h in vaccine analyses. The Vaxx app's Internal Consistency page also plots IPV1 against IPV2, which is not scored. See RMNCAH and vaccine analyses.

sections.heading: Data missingness
sections.text:
- Missing monthly values are measured by 1c: the share of districts with no missing monthly values in a year for any reporting form (see Reporting completeness).
- In the data adjustment step, a missing monthly value is replaced with the district's median monthly value for the year.

sections.heading: Ratio calculations
sections.text:
- ANC1 to Penta1 (3a). Between the first antenatal visit (around 20 weeks of pregnancy) and Penta1 (6-8 weeks after birth), the method assumes a pregnancy loss of 3%, a stillbirth rate of 2%, a twinning rate of 1.5% and neonatal mortality before Penta1 of 3%. With the same survey coverage for ANC1 and Penta1, this gives an expected ANC1 to Penta1 ratio of 1.07; in general the expected ratio is 1.07 × (ANC1 coverage ÷ Penta1 coverage), both from the most recent survey.
- Penta1 to Penta3 (3b). Mortality plays a small role between 6 and 14 weeks of age, so the expected ratio is set by the drop-out between the doses: Penta1 coverage ÷ Penta3 coverage in the latest survey (e.g. 0.95 ÷ 0.85 = 1.12). OPV1 to OPV3 (3c, vaccine analyses) is assessed the same way.
- Acceptable range. A national ratio within ± 0.05 of its expected value is acceptable; outside it, flag the ratio and discuss possible explanations. District ratios vary more: a ratio between 1.0 and 1.5 is considered within range.

sections.heading: Overall quality score
sections.text:
Metric | Numerator | Denominator | Interpretation
Overall score | Computed automatically | Computed automatically | Mean of

1a, 1b, 1c, 2a, 2b

and the district ratio checks (see below)

RMNCAH and vaccine analyses differ here: the district ratio checks in the score are 3c, 3d in RMNCAH analyses and 3f, 3g, 3h in vaccine analyses. In vaccine analyses the score's 1c is the mean over the tracer vaccines (BCG, Penta1-3, OPV1-3, Measles 1) and 2b the mean over the vaccines only; RMNCAH analyses take both over all the indicators. See RMNCAH and vaccine analyses.

The 2024 Countdown vaccination guidebook left 1c out of the score; the apps include it.

sections.heading: Reporting rates
sections.text:
A high national reporting rate can hide many low-reporting districts. Always check the district view and the score by region.

- Reporting rate measures whether reports arrived, not whether the numbers are right. Use outlier detection and internal consistency together.

Sub-national reporting rate heat map

National reporting rate and sub-national units with low reporting

sections.heading: Outliers
sections.text:
Outliers are identified statistically. Always assess whether deviations reflect real-world events (e.g., campaigns) or data errors.

- Expect at least 99% of monthly values (2a), and 90% of districts (2b), to be free of extreme outliers.
- A sudden peak may be a campaign, not an error. Check the trend before you decide.

Outlier detection heat map by region and year

sections.heading: Consistency and ratios
sections.text:
- Reflect on large differences between years (e.g. more than 0.10).
- In a consistency check, points far from the diagonal indicate inconsistent reporting and deserve a look.
- Consistency plots show plausibility, not truth: an unusual Penta1/Penta3 ratio can be a real dropout problem or a data problem.
- The expected ratios come from the survey coverage values, so wrong survey values distort this check.

Consistency checks between ANC1 and Penta1 by year

Ratio plots of ANC1/Penta1 and Penta1/Penta3 by year

sections.heading: Missing values
sections.text: Data missingness heat map by indicator and region

sections.heading: Overall score
sections.text: Overall data quality score table by year

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
- A low score is a reason to investigate, not always to discard a year. Compare with local events before using Remove Years. A year with many outliers or low completeness is a candidate for Remove Years or careful adjustment (see Data adjustment).
- District results are noisier than regional ones because they rest on smaller numbers.
- Changing the performance threshold changes the score, so agree it with your team before comparing years or countries.

sections.heading: Open the data quality pages
sections.text: They are under Data quality in the RMNCAH app and Data Quality Assessment in the Vaxx app: see Data quality for each page and its filters.

sections.heading: Review the metrics
sections.text:
Work through Reporting Rate, Outlier Detection, Data Missingness, Internal Consistency and the Overall Data Quality Score.

DataSuite automatically computes the overall data quality score.

sections.heading: Continue to data preparation
sections.text: Remove unreliable years and adjust the data in Data preparation.

ai.summary: Evaluates health facility data with standard data quality metrics before coverage is estimated: reporting completeness, outlier detection, internal consistency, data missingness, ratio calculations, and an overall quality score.
definitions: 1a: monthly facility reports received / total expected reports (12 x number of facilities) (#reporting-completeness)
1b: districts with at least 90% reporting completeness / total districts (#reporting-completeness)
1c: districts with no missing values across all forms / total districts (#reporting-completeness)

Extreme outlier: a monthly value more than 5 x the median absolute deviation (MAD) from the series' median monthly value (Hampel method); median and MAD from all years except the most recent one (#outlier-detection)
2a: monthly values not classified as outliers / total monthly values; 2b: districts with no outliers / total districts (#outlier-detection)

3a: ANC1/Penta1 reported (national), expected 1.07 x the survey ANC1/Penta1 coverage; 3b: Penta1/Penta3, expected the survey Penta1/Penta3 coverage; vaccine analyses also 3c: OPV1/OPV3 (#internal-consistency)
District ratio checks: share of districts with the ratio between 1.0 and 1.5 -- RMNCAH 3c (ANC1/Penta1), 3d (Penta1/Penta3); vaccine 3f, 3g, 3h (OPV1/OPV3) (#internal-consistency)
Overall score: the mean of 1a, 1b, 1c, 2a, 2b and the district ratio checks -- 3c, 3d (RMNCAH) or 3f, 3g, 3h (vaccine) (#overall-quality-score)
rules: 1a and 1b are the mean over the reporting forms: RMNCAH ANC, delivery, immunization and OPD (not inpatient); vaccine ANC, delivery and immunization (#reporting-completeness)
Missing monthly values are measured by 1c and, in data adjustment, replaced with the district's median monthly value for the year (#data-missingness)
A national ratio within +/- 0.05 of its expected value is acceptable (flag it otherwise); a district ratio of 1.0-1.5 is within range (#ratio-calculations)
The expected ANC1/Penta1 of 1.07 (equal survey coverage) assumes 3% pregnancy loss, 2% stillbirths, 1.5% twins and 3% neonatal mortality before Penta1 (#ratio-calculations)
Internal consistency checks relationships between biologically or programmatically linked indicators, not each indicator alone (#internal-consistency)
interpretation: 1a: 90% or more is good (affects trend interpretation); 1b identifies low-performing districts; 1c how missing values are spread across districts (#reporting-completeness)
2a: 99% or more expected; 2b: 90% or more expected (#outlier-detection)
A high national reporting rate can hide many low-reporting districts (check the district and regional views); it shows reports arrived, not that the numbers are right (#reporting-rates)
Outliers are identified statistically: assess whether a deviation (e.g. a sudden peak) is a real-world event such as a campaign or a data error; check the trend (#outliers)

Points far from the diagonal indicate inconsistent reporting; plots show plausibility, not truth (an unusual Penta1/Penta3 ratio may be real dropout); wrong survey values distort the expected ratios (#consistency-and-ratios)
A low score is a reason to investigate, not always to discard a year; district results are noisier; changing the threshold changes the score (#common-pitfalls)

sections.heading: Denominator assessment and selection
sections.text:
This section on denominator selection helps you select the most appropriate approach for denominator estimation for the computation of the coverage indicators at the national and subnational levels. For more information, please refer to the guidebook on the Countdown DataSuite.

At a glance

- Answers: Which denominator option gives the most plausible coverage, compared with the survey, at national and subnational level?
- Uses: the adjusted numbers from Data adjustment, the UN and DHIS2 population projections, and the survey values (ANC-1 and Penta-1 coverage, stillbirth rate, NMR, PNMR) from Analysis setup.
- Produces: the selected denominator(s) (one or two, depending on the analysis: see Selecting the best denominator option), used for the coverage indicators in Coverage.
- In the apps: Denominators (Denominator Assessment and Denominator Selection).
- Defaults: Defaults and thresholds: denominators

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text:
The numerators of coverage statistics (e.g., number of live births in health facilities) are derived from the health facility data and need to be adjusted as shown in the previous section. The denominator of the coverage statistics (e.g., number of live births in the population) needs to be estimated for national and subnational levels (regions/provinces and districts). Because the numerator comes from facility data and the denominator has to be estimated, the choice of denominator matters as much as the data quality.

For the scientific basis of facility-based coverage and its denominators, see Coverage analysis: rationale.

sections.heading: Service coverage
sections.text: Service coverage is defined as the population who received the service divided by the population who need the services (also referred to as the target population). In a vaccine analysis, it is the number of vaccinated children divided by a target population.

sections.heading: Denominator options
sections.text:
There are six denominator options that are analyzed to determine the most accurate baseline:

- The UN estimates of live births (UN projections)
- The DHIS2 projection of live births (DHIS2 projections)
- Derivation of denominators from ANC-1 services utilization (ANC-1 derived)
- Derivation of denominators from Penta-1 immunization (Penta-1 derived)
- Derivation of denominators from ANC-1 services utilization, with adjustment for annual population growth (ANC-1 population growth)
- Derivation of denominators from Penta-1 immunization, with adjustment for annual population growth (Penta-1 population growth)

In the apps and their data the six are labelled UN projections, DHIS2 projections, ANC1-derived, Penta1-derived, ANC1 population growth and Penta1 population growth, with the ids un, dhis2, anc1, penta1, anc1derived and penta1derived. The ids ending in derived are the population-growth options (5 and 6), not the "-derived" ones (3 and 4): see the Data dictionary.

UN projections are national only. The 2024 Countdown vaccination guidebook: "For the subnational level, no UN projections are available." Below national level, compare the DHIS2 projections and the ANC-1 and Penta-1 derived options. In the apps, the UN projections appear in the national comparison; the denominators you can select are DHIS2, ANC-1, Penta-1, ANC-1 population growth and Penta-1 population growth.

sections.heading: Computing the derived denominators
sections.text:
The ANC-1 derived option starts from the number of women attending a first antenatal visit and works forward through pregnancy to the eligible infants; the Penta-1 derived option starts from the number of infants vaccinated with Penta-1 and works backward.

Population | From ANC-1 | From Penta-1
Pregnancies | ANC-1 ÷ survey ANC-1 coverage | deliveries ÷ (1 − pregnancy loss)
Deliveries | pregnancies × (1 − pregnancy loss) | births × (1 − 0.5 × twin rate)
Births | deliveries ÷ (1 − 0.5 × twin rate) | live births ÷ (1 − stillbirth rate)
Live births | births × (1 − stillbirth rate) | infants ÷ (1 − NMR)
Infants eligible for Penta (under 1) | live births × (1 − NMR) | Penta-1 ÷ survey Penta-1 coverage
Measles 1 target | infants × (1 − PNMR) | infants × (1 − PNMR)
Measles 2 target | infants × (1 − 2 × PNMR) | infants × (1 − 2 × PNMR)

Each coverage indicator uses the population that matches it: pregnancies for ANC, deliveries for institutional deliveries, live births for institutional live births and BCG, infants for Penta, and the measles targets for measles. The DHIS2 and UN projections of live births are converted to the other populations with the same assumptions.

Default assumptions (guidebook):

Assumption | Default
Pregnancy loss | 3%
Stillbirth rate | 2%
Twin rate | 1.5%
Neonatal mortality rate (NMR) | 3%
Post-neonatal mortality rate (PNMR) | 2.4%

The apps use the country's most recent survey values when they are available: ANC-1 and Penta-1 coverage (otherwise 98% and 97%), and the stillbirth rate, NMR and PNMR. When the survey gives no NMR, the apps use 2.5%, not the guidebook's 3%. Pregnancy loss and the twin rate always use the defaults.

sections.heading: Selecting the best denominator option
sections.text:
The goal here is to identify the best denominator option for the computation of the coverage indicators. How many denominators you choose depends on the analysis.

RMNCAH and vaccine analyses differ here: a vaccine analysis uses one denominator for all the immunization indicators (the Vaxx app's Vaccination denominator); an RMNCAH analysis uses two: a maternal denominator for the ANC and delivery indicators and an immunization denominator for the immunization indicators (the RMNCAH app's Maternal denominator and Vaccination denominator). See RMNCAH and vaccine analyses.

To identify the best option, follow these steps: (1) the population trend comparison, below; then, under Interpretation, (2) the denominator selection examination and (3) the final selection and synthesis.

sections.heading: Population trend comparison
sections.text:
Under the "Population Trend" section, compare the trends in the total population, total live births, and under-1 population between the UN and the DHIS2 projections.

Select the indicator trends (total population, live births, or under-1 population) that are consistent across the two sources, with estimates generally close: the two sources are close and follow the same direction, with a stable, plausible gap between UN and DHIS2.

- Example: You may select the under-1 population if the UN estimates and the DHIS2 projections for that demographic are very close.

Population comparison between UN and DHIS2 projections

The indicator selected in this step sets the DHIS2 population the derived denominators are built from, and will be used to adjust the ANC-1-derived and Penta-1-derived options with population growth.

Check the quality of the DHIS2 projections. The guidebook flags a DHIS2 projection as inconsistent when:

- Over time: the population growth rate or the crude birth rate (CBR) changes by 2 per 1,000 or more between years.
- Against the UN projections: the population differs by more than 5% (relative difference), the growth rate by more than 0.3% (absolute difference), or the CBR by more than 5 per 1,000.
- Implied crude death rate: CDR = CBR − growth rate is negative or below 5 per 1,000.

The apps show the trends; these checks are made by the analyst.

sections.heading: Reading the population trends
sections.text:
- Large gaps between UN and DHIS2 suggest an outdated census base or a wrong population entry in the workbook.
- A sudden break in one line usually means a change in how the population was projected, not a real change in births.
- DHIS2 projections often drift when they are based on an old census.

sections.heading: Denominator selection examination
sections.text:
Under "Denominator Selection", examine the consistency between the survey estimates and the computed estimate from DHIS2 data using each denominator method. This is done by comparing three sets of graphs at national and subnational levels:

a. Comparison of national estimates: First, compare the national estimate of each indicator between the routine data and the survey data by examining the first bar graph for the survey year. The figure shows a horizontal dotted line indicating the survey estimate and a bar corresponding to the routine estimate. A denominator that gives coverage close to the survey, without exceeding 100 percent, is a good candidate. In making this comparison, note down the best denominator options (there may be more than one viable option).

National coverage by denominator option compared with the survey estimate

b. Subnational level comparison on the survey year: In the second set of figures, the horizontal bars represent the coverage estimate from the routine data compared to the "diamond" which represents the survey estimate. A figure is produced for each denominator option. Review each figure and identify the best denominator option based on the closeness of the coverage estimate from the survey to that of the routine data. Look for the option that agrees best with the survey across regions. Similarly, examine estimates that are implausible (e.g., coverage estimates above 100%, or far above it). Note down the best denominator option.

c. Trends in national estimates: Examine the trend estimate for each denominator option by looking for consistency and overall plausibility in the historical trends: plausible, smooth trends.

National coverage over time by denominator option

The survey is the gold standard. The guidebook compares the coverage of institutional live births and Penta-3 from each option with the most recent survey, and selects the method with the smallest absolute difference between the routine and survey coverage, at national and subnational level.

sections.heading: Final selection and synthesis
sections.text:
Combine your notes from sub-steps (a), (b), and (c) above to select the best-performing denominator (one or two, depending on the analysis: see Selecting the best denominator option).

Summarize your choice in a short paragraph, documenting the justification for each denominator you selected.

- The best denominator is not the one that gives the highest coverage, but the one that best agrees with (is closest to) the survey and stays stable and consistent over time.
- Denominators derived from ANC 1 or Penta 1 assume that most of the population attends the service and that facilities report completely. They are weakest where reporting is poor; if results look odd, go back to Data quality.
- Sub-national denominators can be less reliable than national ones. Read them together with district data quality.

A denominator derived from Penta1 makes Penta1 coverage look near 100 percent by construction. Judge it on Penta3 and Measles 1, and against the survey.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
- Comparing against the survey when the survey year is far from the analysis years. Weigh that in your judgement.
- Choosing a denominator per chart instead of once for the whole analysis. The denominator you select changes every coverage, inequality, target, mortality and health system result.

sections.heading: Assess the population trends
sections.text: On Denominator Assessment (Population Trend in the Vaxx app), compare the UN and DHIS2 projections and select the best population (see Denominator Assessment).

sections.heading: Compare the denominator options
sections.text: On Denominator Selection, compare coverage under each option with the survey, nationally, subnationally and over time (see Denominator Selection).

sections.heading: Choose the denominator
sections.text: Set the denominator(s) the rest of the analysis uses (see Choose the denominator).

pages.title: Planning for dissemination, decisions and action

sections.heading: Planning for dissemination, decisions and action
sections.text:
The objective of the final session of the workshop is to identify concrete actions to take forward the work you have completed. As you have been preparing and interpreting your analyses, you have been encouraged to think about the full cycle of data-driven decision-making.

At a glance

- Answers: Who will use the findings, for which questions, and which concrete actions will take the work forward?
- Uses: the analysis, interpretation and key findings from the previous steps (see the end-to-end workflow).
- Produces: information products and dissemination strategies tailored to users, and actions for data use, capacity building and further analysis.
- In the apps: Reports and Exports, reports and AI.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text:
Cycle of data-driven decision-making

This starts with identifying the data users and understanding the questions or issues they aim to address, and then preparing the analysis, interpretation and key findings that would be most useful for addressing those questions or issues.

Information products and dissemination strategies should be tailored to align with users' preferences and should be supplemented with support to decision-makers in using the analysis and following up on agreed actions.

sections.heading: Key considerations
sections.text:
- Identify use cases and audiences
- Use appropriate dissemination platforms
- Integrate into routine decision-making forums
- Link to Ministry of Health reviews and reporting processes

sections.heading: Purpose of the activity
sections.text: These activities outline how analysis outputs can be translated into action, capacity strengthening, and further research within the CD2030 framework.

sections.heading: Supporting data use and action
sections.text:
View examples

- Present findings, interpretation and key insights to the country RMNCAH platform and related technical working groups for them to review and interpret. Support them to identify opportunities to take action based on data and evidence - for example, address gender or geographic inequities, test pilots with implementation research or evaluation, advocate for policy change or resources, etc.
- Include analysis as part of evidence base to inform the development of new RMNCAH-N strategy, a mid-term review and an evaluation, if any of these are underway.
- Produce an article or analytical brief for targeted audiences with key learning, takeaways, and proposed actions following the workshop, as an entry point for follow-up.

sections.heading: Building capacity
sections.text:
View examples

- Carry out cascade training at national and district levels on the concepts, interpretation, and use of specific analyses, through the country Countdown collaboration.
- Hold sessions to sensitize national bureau of statistics staff on Countdown methodology to build ownership.
- Share the concepts and findings of health facility data quality assessment with HMIS and M&E staff to build their understanding and as an opportunity for strengthening routine systems for data quality.
- Build HMIS and M&E staff capacity to understand the relevance of gender and equity-related indicators and analyses.
- Build capacity of staff to incorporate some of the new analytical techniques and approaches into dashboards, policy briefs, statistical reports, etc.

sections.heading: Identifying needs for further analysis
sections.text:
View examples

- Identify opportunities for implementation research to address bottlenecks or to inform potential scale-up/replication of successes based on findings from the analysis.
- Identify opportunities for further research or analysis in order to better understand trends in gender and equity that were observed in the analysis and to inform options for action.

sections.heading: Information products
sections.text:
Two products of the apps' standard reports are the ones most stakeholders ask for:

- The synthesis chartbook is the complete analysis in one document for the review meeting.
- The sub-national one-pager gives each region its own statistical profile.

What each standard report contains, and how to build it, is in Reports.

sections.heading: Preparing reports for stakeholders
sections.text:
- Settle data quality, adjustment and the denominators (in the Vaxx App, the denominator) before you generate the synthesis, and state them in a text block on the first page.
- Answer every interpretation prompt or delete it. Leaving prompts in is the most common reason a chartbook looks unfinished.
- Fill in the cover: title, editors, date and logos of the partners.
- Produce the report in the language of the audience, and use Print layout before you send a PDF.
- Duplicate the one-pager for each region and share the PowerPoint files with the regional teams (for the Vaxx App, also the immunization managers).
- Link findings to actions: see Supporting data use and action.

sections.heading: Sharing charts and tables
sections.text: Download the data with the plot when you share a chart. The Excel file carries the title and the numbers, so readers can check the figure.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text: - Sharing a chart without its data or the denominator. Always state the denominator and adjustment used.

sections.heading: In the apps
sections.text: The apps turn the analysis into products you can share.

sections.heading: Build a report
sections.text: The Reports page in the Output section builds Word or PDF documents and PowerPoint or PDF slide decks from the loaded dataset. Standard reports contain prompts headed Notes or Interpretations: replace them with the interpretation agreed at your review meeting. See Reports.

sections.heading: Export charts, tables and datasets
sections.text: Download single charts, tables and datasets, or ask the DataSuite chat assistant about the saved dataset. See Exports, reports and AI.
