sections.heading: Equity assessment (equiplots)
sections.text:
National coverage averages mask critical disparities that determine whether health systems are truly leaving no one behind. This module uses household survey data to assess inequalities across three major dimensions: residence (urban/rural), wealth (richest-to-poorest quintiles), and maternal education. By visualizing coverage trajectories separately for each population subgroup alongside the national trend, equiplots reveal whether gaps are narrowing or widening—essential information for targeting health investments equitably.

At a glance

- Answers: Are coverage gaps between population subgroups (urban/rural residence, household wealth quintile, mother's education) narrowing or widening, and which type of inequality do the wealth quintiles show?
- Uses: household survey data on area of residence, household wealth quintiles and the mother's education, with the national coverage trend for comparison (National coverage).
- Produces: equiplots of each subgroup's coverage over time alongside the national trend, and the inequality pattern (top, linear or bottom inequality) for wealth. Next: Subnational analysis.
- In the apps: Equity Assessment (in the Vaxx app, the Survey Data page under National Inequality).

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text:
Three distinct inequality patterns emerge from the data: top inequality (only the rich escape), linear inequality (wealth-associated gradients), and bottom inequality (poorest left behind). Each pattern signals different programming priorities: mass access campaigns, pro-poor targeting, or education initiatives respectively. Tracking these patterns over time reveals whether equity interventions work and whether your health system is progressing toward universal coverage for all population groups, not just national averages.

The scientific basis is set out in the rationale.

sections.heading: Rationale and approach
sections.text:
Scientific basis for the analysis:

Household surveys provide critical information on inequalities. Our focus is on three major dimensions of inequality: area of residence, wealth and education.

For area of residence, we focus on urban/rural areas, for wealth, we use household wealth quintiles and for education we focus on education of the mother. Equiplots are used to assess whether the country has made progress since 2010 in reducing the poor-rich gap or the gap between women with no education or low education and women with higher education.

For wealth quintiles, it can be assessed what the type of inequality is, as all categories are of the same size. Each pattern requires a different strategy of health programming and targeting:

- Top inequality (mass deprivation): If the richest are well ahead of all other wealth quintiles, only the rich escape.
- Linear inequality: If the coverage differences are equidistant, this is a linear pattern where the increasing household wealth is linearly associated with higher coverage.
- Bottom inequality (marginalization): If the poorest are left behind, this means marginalization of the poorest.

sections.heading: Interpretation of equiplots
sections.text:
See the rationale: Equity analysis (equiplots).

The interpretation should focus on whether inequalities have reduced over time and to what extent global targets for coverage have been met. Consider your audience(s) and what key messages and insights you want to get across.

The following questions should guide and be answered by the interpretation:

- What is the level of inequality in the most recent data point?
- How have inequalities changed over time?
- Is there any inequality pattern that can be observed?
- What will be the best approaches to reduce inequalities?

How to read an equiplot:

- The distance between the points is the inequality.
- For wealth, read the pattern: only the richest ahead means top inequality, evenly spaced groups mean linear inequality, and the poorest far behind means bottom inequality (marginalisation). Each calls for a different programme response.
- Focus on the latest data point, the change since 2010 and whether the gap is closing.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text: - Equity charts come from survey files and can be several years old. Compare them with routine trends, not with a single year of DHIS2 data.

sections.heading: Health system performance
sections.text:
This section focuses on analyzing health systems performance, including the availability and quality of health services, the health workforce, and health financing. The analysis aims to identify gaps and challenges in the health system that may affect the delivery of reproductive, maternal, newborn, child, adolescent health, and nutrition (RMNCAH-N) services.

It contains the following subsections:

- Health system inputs (national and subnational)
- Health system outputs (national and subnational)
- Private sector and RMNCAH-N services

At a glance

- Answers: Where do high health system inputs fail to translate into RMNCAH-N service coverage, and which regions deliver services efficiently?
- Uses: health system inputs (infrastructure, workforce and, where available, financing) at national and Admin1 level; under-5 OPD visits and hospital admissions from service utilization; institutional live birth coverage from a recent household survey or the preferred DHIS2 estimate (national coverage).
- Produces: input indicators checked against benchmarks, and descriptive comparisons of outputs by inputs across Admin1 units, for planning dissemination, decisions and action.
- In the apps: Service utilization and health system (RMNCAH app only).

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The scientific basis for comparing health system inputs with outputs is set out in the rationale: health systems performance.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: The core objective remains isolating specific sub-national bottlenecks where high system inputs fail to translate into expected RMNCAH-N service coverage outputs, or conversely, identifying high-performing regions exhibiting strong service delivery efficiency.

sections.heading: Analytical scope
sections.text: The analytical scope is restricted to a direct, descriptive comparison of health system outputs (coverage of tracer interventions) against system inputs (infrastructure, workforce, and financing metrics) at the sub-national tier (Admin1 level). More complex methodologies, such as data envelopment analysis, frontier efficiency modeling, or composite indexing controlling for multi-sectoral socioeconomic development factors, fall outside the scope of this operational section.

sections.heading: Health systems inputs evaluation framework
sections.text:
First, the assessment focuses on the quality of data for the health system indicators at both national and sub-national levels. For selected indicators, the evaluation must target:

- Global benchmarking: Comparison with global data repositories for selected indicators (national level only).
- Plausibility auditing: Assessing the plausibility of indicator values across sub-national units to identify major outliers or improbable patterns.

In addition, it is highly useful to explore the cross-correlations of health system inputs with one another (e.g., workforce density plotted against inpatient bed capacity). This correlation mapping is effective for detecting systemic data inconsistencies across Admin1 units (provinces, regions, or counties).

Finally, assessing the alignment of health system performance metrics across different administrative levels (e.g., comparing Admin1 aggregates directly against nested district values) helps isolate structural anomalies, reporting discrepancies, or geographical outliers.

sections.heading: Health financing
sections.text:
Health financing indicators at the district or Admin1 levels are difficult to obtain and are frequently limited to budgeted allocations rather than actual expenditures. These datasets also tend to capture government resources exclusively, missing out on external donor aid, private insurance, or out-of-pocket spending.

System rule: These financial tracking data are not loaded as default parameters here. However, if reliable sub-national expenditure data are available to the country team, they should be utilized to enrich the health system inputs baseline.

sections.heading: Core health professionals per 10,000 population
sections.text:
Health workforce trackers are often of poor data quality and can be operationally difficult to extract. The primary indicator used by the platform is the density of core health professionals per 10,000 population. This cohort includes:

- Physicians (medical doctors)
- Non-physician clinicians (e.g., clinical officers or health officers with surgical training and multi-year certifications, but lacking a full academic medical degree)
- Professional nurses
- Certified midwives

Density threshold benchmarks:

- Historical threshold (2006 WHO guidance): A minimum baseline of 23 core health professionals per 10,000 population was designated as the critical tipping point required to achieve the skilled birth attendance volumes necessary to reduce maternal and child mortality.
- Modern threshold (UHC era): Updated global targets establish a significantly higher baseline of at least 44.5 core health professionals per 10,000 population to successfully achieve Universal Health Coverage (UHC) goals.

Health workforce density per 10,000 population by Admin1 unit

sections.heading: Number of health facilities per 10,000 population
sections.text:
This metric serves as a baseline indicator of physical health infrastructure and includes all tiers of care: hospitals, comprehensive health centers, and lower-level primary points of care such as health posts and dispensaries. Both private and public sectors must be accounted for.

$\text{Health Facility Density} = \left( \frac{\text{Total Number of Health Facilities}}{\text{Total Population}} \right) \times 10{,}000$

This is a crude indicator because it weighs small primary dispensaries identically to tertiary referral hospitals.

Indicative benchmark: A value of 2 facilities per 10,000 population is used as an indicative reference baseline. A sub-national unit dropping below 2 is categorized as having low infrastructure access.

sections.heading: Number of hospitals per 100,000 population
sections.text:
To gain specific insights into the infrastructure capacity available for acute inpatient services, the platform computes the density of hospitals scaled per 100,000 individuals:

$\text{Hospital Density} = \left( \frac{\text{Total Number of Hospitals}}{\text{Total Population}} \right) \times 100{,}000$

sections.heading: Inpatient bed density per 10,000 population
sections.text:
This indicator serves as an additional measure of structural healthcare capacity and is calculated as the absolute number of official inpatient beds across all functioning health facilities per 10,000 population.

$\text{Inpatient Bed Density} = \left( \frac{\text{Total Inpatient Beds}}{\text{Total Population}} \right) \times 10{,}000$

Sub-national health system tab showing facility density per 10,000 population by Admin1 unit

sections.heading: Benchmarks drawn in the apps
sections.text:
The Sub-National Health System charts draw a benchmark for three indicators, and each region is coloured Meets benchmark or Below benchmark:

Indicator | Benchmark
Health facility density | 2 per 10,000
Inpatient bed density | 25 per 10,000
Workforce density | 44.5 per 10,000
Hospital density | No benchmark

sections.heading: Health systems outputs by inputs at the sub-national level
sections.text: The second part of the analysis explores the statistical association between health system inputs and matching service utilization or coverage indicators across sub-national units (Admin1 level). The following associations are evaluated:

sections.heading: Inpatient infrastructure and under-5 hospital admissions
sections.text:
The platform evaluates the association between hospital density (per 100,000 population) or inpatient bed density (per 10,000 population) plotted against the annual hospital admission rates for children under 5, stratified by Admin1 unit.

- Theoretical expectation: We expect that regions with lower hospital or bed density will exhibit lower pediatric admission rates, while regions with higher structural capacity will show higher admission rates. Visually, this trend should reflect a positive slope on a linear regression line.
- Identifying and interpreting outliers: When reviewing the scatter plot, teams must look for major outliers, such as regions with very low infrastructure density but unusually high pediatric admission rates. Potential operational explanations include:
  
  - Infrastructure under-reporting: Active hospitals or bed capacities are under-reported in the system by these specific regions.
  - High clinical throughput: The existing hospitals in these low-density regions operate at exceptionally high admission turnover and bed occupancy rates.
  - Numerator inflation: Hospital admissions are over-reported or double-counted in these areas.

The technical narrative should be based on contextual knowledge of the actual situation in these sub-national units.

sections.heading: Health workforce density and under-5 outpatient utilization
sections.text:
This model checks the association between health workforce density (core health professionals per 10,000 population) and the mean number of outpatient department (OPD) visits among children under 5, by region.

- Theoretical expectation: We expect that regions with lower health workforce density will have lower OPD utilization rates for children, and those with a higher workforce density will have higher utilization rates. This relationship is demonstrated by a positive slope on a linear regression line.
- Identifying and interpreting outliers: If a region displays low health workforce density alongside high OPD utilization rates, the country team should evaluate whether:
  
  - Workforce under-reporting: The count of core health professionals is under-reported by these regions.
  - High staff workload: Health workers in these areas experience an exceptionally high clinical workload and patient volume.
  - Numerator inflation: OPD visits are over-reported due to data quality or documentation issues.

The final interpretation must reconcile these data points with the ground reality of the affected regions.

sections.heading: Health workforce density and institutional live birth coverage
sections.text:
This component cross-tabulates health workforce density (core health professionals per 10,000 population) against institutional live birth coverage by region. For delivery coverage inputs, teams can utilize data from a recent household survey or the preferred DHIS2 facility-derived estimate.

- Theoretical expectation: We expect that regions with lower health workforce density will experience lower institutional delivery coverage rates, while those with a higher concentration of core professionals will show higher coverage. This will reflect a positive slope on a linear regression line.

The structural and data-quality considerations for interpreting outliers in this model match the analytical steps outlined in the sections above.

PHC performance tab plotting facility density against the PHC index by Admin1 unit

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
- Comparing health system densities with different denominators or population years.
- Treating a benchmark as a target for every region. It is a reference, and context matters.
- Interpreting a quadrant position as cause and effect. A comparison of inputs with a service index, as in PHC Performance, is descriptive, not proof of efficiency.

No benchmark for hospital density (#benchmarks-drawn-in-the-apps)

sections.heading: Framework overview
sections.text:
This page summarizes the CD2030 DataSuite analytical framework.
It is intended to help teams move from raw facility and survey data to defensible national and sub-national coverage findings.

The CD2030 DataSuite implements an end-to-end analytical workflow that transforms raw health facility data into credible, actionable coverage estimates.
The workflow follows a logical sequence: assess data quality, correct for incompleteness and errors, select evidence-based denominators, calculate coverage, and examine inequality patterns at national and geographic levels.

Countdown analysis workflow

This structured approach addresses a universal challenge in RMNCAH monitoring: facility data are abundant but often unreliable, while surveys provide gold-standard coverage estimates but are infrequent and expensive.
The CD2030 DataSuite bridges this gap by systematically vetting facility data, calibrating them against survey benchmarks, and producing continuous trend lines with quantified uncertainty.
The result is confidence that your coverage numbers reflect reality rather than data artifacts.

sections.heading: End-to-end workflow
sections.text:
The framework follows a practical sequence:

- Load and configure facility and survey data.
- Calibrate key national benchmark rates.
- Assess data quality before estimating coverage.
- Adjust incomplete, unstable, or unreliable data.
- Select the best-performing denominator.
- Generate and interpret coverage (including Bayesian coverage estimation), equity, sub-national, mortality, service utilization and health system performance results, in that order.
- Plan dissemination, decisions and action.

In the apps, the same sequence is followed page by page: see Analysis steps (RMNCAH app).

sections.heading: Framework modules
sections.text: The final purpose of the framework is practical use. Findings should inform country review processes, planning discussions, and technical working groups so that the analysis leads to concrete RMNCAH action rather than standing alone as a report.

sections.heading: Mortality
sections.text:
This step asks whether the maternal deaths, stillbirths and neonatal deaths reported by health facilities are plausible, and how complete facility death reporting is. It produces the institutional mortality rates (iMMR, iSBR and neonatal deaths before discharge), data quality checks, and modelled completeness of facility reporting.

At a glance

- Answers: Are the institutional mortality rates plausible? Is under-reporting more likely for stillbirths or for maternal deaths? How complete is the facilities' reporting of deaths?
- Uses: the unadjusted reported deaths and births/live births in health facilities (no data adjustment for reporting rates or outliers), and population mortality estimates (UN estimates, or a recent national survey or census).
- Produces: iMMR, iSBR and neonatal deaths before discharge by region and year, data quality flags, and the completeness of facility reporting across modelled scenarios; used in the Mortality report (Reports).
- In the apps: Mortality (RMNCAH app only).
- Defaults: Mortality

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Maternal deaths and stillbirths are few and fluctuate, and low institutional mortality in less-developed regions is more likely to signal under-reporting than better outcomes. Checking the rates for plausibility, and comparing them with population estimates, shows how complete facility reporting is before the rates are used. The scientific basis is in Rationale: institutional mortality.

sections.heading: Institutional mortality in the CD2030 analytical approach
sections.text:
The definitions for institutional, community, and population maternal mortality and for stillbirths are outlined in the matrix below.

Indicator | Numerator | Denominator
Institutional maternal mortality ratio (iMMR) | Number of maternal deaths in health facilities | $\frac{\text{Number of live births in health facilities}}{\text{100,000}}$
Population maternal mortality (MMR) | Number of maternal deaths in the population | $\frac{\text{Number of live births in the population}}{\text{100,000}}$
Community maternal mortality ratio (cMMR) | Number of maternal deaths in the community | $\frac{\text{Number of live births in the community}}{\text{100,000}}$
Institutional stillbirth rate (iSBR) | Number of stillbirths in health facilities | $\frac{\text{Number of births in health facilities}}{\text{1,000}}$
Population stillbirth rate (SBR) | Number of stillbirths in the population | $\frac{\text{Number of births in the population}}{\text{1,000}}$
Community stillbirth rate (cSBR) | Number of stillbirths in the community | $\frac{\text{Number of births in the community}}{\text{1,000}}$
Neonatal mortality (before discharge) | Number of neonatal deaths before discharge | $\frac{\text{Number of live births in health facilities}}{\text{1,000}}$

sections.heading: iMMR and iSBR review
sections.text:
The annual mortality rates are computed using the unadjusted data on reported deaths and births/live births in health facilities.
We do not adjust for reporting rates and outliers (as is done for other interventions) because it is difficult to adjust maternal deaths and stillbirths, where the number of deaths is small and fluctuating.

It is however advisable to check the data for any extreme outliers in the annual data (e.g., numbers of deaths that clearly indicate data entry errors) and replace these with the average of the surrounding years.

sections.heading: Ratio of stillbirths to maternal deaths at national level
sections.text:
We expect maternal mortality and stillbirth to be positively correlated given the commonalities in causes.
Based on a review of the global estimates, historical data, and health facility studies, we expect the ratio of stillbirth to maternal death to be in the range of 5 to 25 for countries in sub-Saharan Africa.
We compute the ratio as the number of reported stillbirths divided by the number of reported maternal deaths in DHIS2 or MPDSR, in a specific time period (usually a year) and raise a "data quality flag" if the ratio is outside the 5-25 range.

sections.heading: Expected ranges on the DQA charts
sections.text:
The Institutional Mortality DQA charts in the apps check three ratios, each against an expected range, and show the median:

Check | What it measures | Expected range
Fresh stillbirths | Fresh stillbirths as a percentage of all stillbirths | 30 to 55
Stillbirth to maternal death ratio | Stillbirths per maternal death | 6 to 15
Neonatal / maternal deaths | Institutional neonatal deaths per maternal death | 5 to 10

The stillbirth-to-maternal-death band on the chart (6 to 15) is narrower than the range used to flag national data (5 to 25, see Ratio of stillbirths to maternal deaths at national level); the question in the Mortality report asks whether the ratio is in the range of 5 to 15. The three values are the apps' as they stand.

sections.heading: Consistency of iMMR with population and community estimates
sections.text:
The completeness of reporting by health facilities can be estimated by comparing the reported iMMR based on facility data with an expected iMMR.
The population MMR, community MMR, and iMMR must be mathematically consistent.
While variations will occur between different populations, it is statistically improbable to observe a community MMR of 1,000 when the institutional MMR is reported at 100.

An expected MMR in health facilities can be modeled based on two primary sets of parameters:

- Maternal mortality ratio in the whole population ($M_p$): This accounts for both community and institutional deaths. Teams can utilize the lower bound, median, or upper bounds of global estimates for each country (e.g., UN estimates), or results from a recent national household survey.
- Ratio of community to institutional maternal mortality ($\frac{M_c}{M_i}$): This model evaluates assumptions ranging from 0.5 (where community MMR is half the institutional MMR) through 1.0 (where they are equal) up to 2.0 (where $M_c$ is twice $M_i$). The selection of this ratio depends on the local proportion of births occurring in health facilities ($P_i$). Evidence suggests that the community-to-institutional ratio tends to expand as institutional birth rates and overall facility utilization rates increase.

sections.heading: Mathematical modeling and formulations
sections.text:
The total population MMR ($M_p$) represents the sum of the institutional and community mortality ratios, weighted by the proportion of live births occurring in each respective setting:

$M_p = (M_i \times P_i) + (M_c \times (1 - P_i))$

Where:

- $M_p$: Maternal mortality ratio in the population
- $M_i$: Institutional maternal mortality ratio
- $M_c$: Maternal mortality ratio in the community
- $P_i$: The proportion of live births occurring in a health institution

sections.heading: Back-calculating community mortality
sections.text:
Given that $M_i$ is derived from raw DHIS2 data and $M_p$ is provided by independent UN population estimates, the true community MMR ($M_c$) can be isolated and solved as:

$M_c = \frac{M_p - (M_i \times P_i)}{1 - P_i}$

Example: If $M_i = 100$, $M_c = 200$, and $75\%$ of births take place within health facilities ($P_i = 0.75$), the absolute population MMR is calculated as:

$M_p = (100 \times 0.75) + (200 \times 0.25) = 75 + 50 = 125$

In this scenario, the community-to-institutional mortality ratio ($\frac{M_c}{M_i}$) equals $\frac{200}{100} = 2.0$.

sections.heading: Calculating expected institutional mortality
sections.text:
Conversely, if we establish a baseline estimate for the population MMR ($M_p$) and assume a specific community-to-institutional variance ratio ($R = \frac{M_c}{M_i}$), we can calculate the mathematically expected institutional MMR using the following formula:

$\text{Expected } M_i = \frac{M_p}{P_i + \left( \frac{M_c}{M_i} \times (1 - P_i) \right)}$

Example: If $75\%$ of women deliver in health facilities ($P_i = 0.75$), the true population $M_p$ is known to be 200, and the assumed community-to-institutional ratio ($\frac{M_c}{M_i}$) is 2, the expected institutional MMR is:

$\text{Expected } M_i = \frac{200}{0.75 + (2 \times 0.25)} = \frac{200}{1.25} = 160$

sections.heading: Computing reporting completeness
sections.text:
Finally, the estimated level of completeness of facility reporting is calculated by dividing the raw reported $iMMR$ (from DHIS2) by the expected $iMMR$:

$\text{Completeness of Facility Reporting} = \frac{\text{Reported } M_i}{\text{Expected } M_i}$

Example: If the raw reported MMR in DHIS2 was 100, but the modeled expected MMR was 160, the final facility reporting completeness level is:

$\text{Completeness} = \frac{100}{160} = 62.5\%$

sections.heading: Methodological footnotes and technical definitions
sections.text: This section compiles the core clinical definitions, mathematical assumptions, and data-cleaning guardrails referenced throughout the institutional mortality and data quality modules.

sections.heading: Maternal death
sections.text: Definition: The death of a woman from any cause related to or aggravated by pregnancy or its management (excluding accidental or incidental causes) during pregnancy and childbirth or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, irrespective of the duration and site of the pregnancy.

sections.heading: Stillbirth
sections.text:
Definition: A baby who dies after 28 weeks of pregnancy (gestation), but before or during birth.

Classification: Clinical records typically distinguish between:

- Ante-partum stillbirths (macerated): Deaths occurring before the onset of labor, showing signs of tissue deterioration.
- Intra-partum stillbirths (fresh): Deaths occurring during labor or delivery.

The figure below shows the institutional fresh stillbirths as a percentage of total stillbirths by region (dots) and the national median (red line), with the plausible range of 30% to 55% marked by dashed lines.

Institutional fresh stillbirths as a percentage of total stillbirths

sections.heading: Outlier detection thresholds
sections.text:
While annual mortality inputs are generally kept unadjusted due to small, fluctuating case numbers, users must manually inspect the raw data for extreme entry errors. Outliers are defined using two statistical thresholds:

- Any annual data point deviating by more than 3 standard deviations ($\sigma$) from the long-term annual mean.
- Any monthly data point exceeding 5 times the Median Absolute Deviation ($MAD$) from the calculated baseline median.

sections.heading: Community-to-institutional MMR ratios
sections.text:
The baseline ratios ($\frac{M_c}{M_i}$) pre-configured into the modeling engine (0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0) are derived from empirical field studies. These studies cross-referenced institutional deaths against total population mortality estimates, accounting for:

- The absolute proportion of all national maternal deaths that occurred within formal health infrastructure.
- The matching percentage of total births that took place inside health facilities.

sections.heading: MPDSR vs. all-cause facility reporting
sections.text:
A primary structural factor skewing institutional maternal mortality ratios ($iMMR$) is the physical location of the death within a hospital complex:

- If data collection relies strictly on Maternity Ward logs or Maternal and Perinatal Death Surveillance and Response (MPDSR) audits, deaths occurring upon clinical re-admission or outside the labor ward (e.g., intensive care, emergency blocks, or general surgical wards due to post-abortal sepsis or delayed hemorrhage) are frequently omitted.
- If the data engine draws from a comprehensive, facility-wide all-cause mortality registry where underlying maternal causes are accurately coded, this systemic under-reporting bias is mitigated.

sections.heading: Considerations for iMMR
sections.text:
The figure below displays the institutional maternal mortality per 100,000 live births for regions (dots) and for the country as a whole (line and annual values) by year.

Institutional maternal mortality per 100,000 live births by region and year

When interpreting the institutional maternal mortality ratio (iMMR), several critical data quality and structural considerations must be made:

- Extreme high outliers: Assess if there are any extreme outliers on the high side that may be due to major data entry errors. These should be flagged for potential correction or exclusion.
- Implausibly low rates: Identify how many regions have an implausibly low $iMMR$, which is arbitrarily defined as less than 25 per 100,000 live births (25 is roughly two times the average MMR in high-income countries of 12.5).
- Contextual validation: Determine if these low-rate regions are more advanced areas where lower mortality is demographically expected, or if they are less-developed regions. Low mortality in less-developed regions strongly indicates a major under-reporting of institutional deaths rather than superior clinical outcomes.

To complement this analysis, a geographic mapping of the indicator is highly recommended.

sections.heading: Geographic distribution
sections.text:
A map displaying the $iMMR$ by region is a useful addition to guide the interpretation of the data, helping teams quickly focus on spatial patterns and identify potential under-reporting or data quality issues across sub-national units.

Map of the institutional maternal mortality ratio by region

High values on a map are not always high mortality. Regions with few births can swing widely, and regions that report well can look worse than regions that under-report.

sections.heading: Considerations for iSBR
sections.text:
The figure below presents the stillbirth rate per 1,000 births for regions and the country, using the same format as for maternal mortality.

Institutional stillbirth rate per 1,000 births by region and year

When analyzing the institutional stillbirth rate (iSBR), the written interpretation should explicitly address the following evaluation questions:

- Implausibly low rates: How many regions have an implausibly low iSBR, which is defined as less than 6 per 1,000 births (6 is approximately two times the average SBR in high-income countries)?
- Data quality vs. development: Are these identified areas more advanced regions where mortality is expected to be lower due to better clinical infrastructure, or is this a clear sign of major under-reporting of deaths in less-developed regions of the country?

In addition, the institutional mortality levels can be compared to the most recent mortality estimates for the population. These population estimates could be coming from a recent national survey or census, or we can use the UN estimates for maternal mortality (for 2020) and stillbirth rates (for 2021).

This is to obtain an idea of the difference between the institutional mortality and the population mortality. Interpretation should seek to explain:

- How far is the iMMR (or iSBR) from the UN estimates of the population mortality, including the uncertainty range of the global estimates: this difference will be used further to assess the data quality.

The institutional neonatal mortality rates (per 1,000 live births) based on reported neonatal deaths may also be graphed similar to iMMR and iSBR, but have to be interpreted with additional caution. Almost all babies stay at least 24 hours after delivery in the hospital but after that many are discharged and the observation time in health facilities is variable. Therefore, the statistic is mostly referred to as neonatal deaths before discharge per 1,000 live births, which includes day 1, some deaths on day 2, fewer deaths on day 3 etc. Because they are deaths of live-born babies before discharge, they understate community neonatal mortality.

A rough guide to assess reporting completeness is that expected mortality of neonatal deaths before discharge in health facilities should be at least half of neonatal mortality in the population. So for instance, if population neonatal mortality is 20 per 1,000 live births, we expect institutional neonatal mortality at least 10 per 1,000 live births in the health facilities.

Institutional neonatal deaths before discharge per 1,000 live births

sections.heading: Stillbirth to maternal death ratio
sections.text:
Interpretation:

- If the ratio is lower than 5: under-reporting of stillbirths is likely greater than under-reporting of maternal deaths.
- If the ratio is equal or greater than 25: under-reporting of maternal deaths is likely to be the main issue, under-reporting of stillbirth less serious than for maternal deaths.
- If the ratio is between 5 and 25: under-reporting of maternal deaths and under-reporting of stillbirths are both possible, or reporting of both is of good quality (this requires that the level is also in the expected range - component 1).

Ratio of stillbirths to maternal deaths in health facilities

sections.heading: Reading the DQA checks
sections.text:
How to read the expected ranges on the DQA charts:

- A very low maternal mortality ratio with a low stillbirth-to-maternal-death ratio can point to under-reporting of deaths, not to good care.
- A share of fresh stillbirths far outside its range suggests that fresh and macerated stillbirths are misclassified.
- Regions that sit outside the range in every year are the priority for data review.

sections.heading: Evaluation scenarios and interpretation
sections.text:
DataSuite models completeness of reporting across multiple scenarios simultaneously.
The diagnostic chart below illustrates reporting completeness across three distinct population MMR levels (lower bound, median/best estimate, and upper bound) mapped against a varying range of community-to-institutional mortality ratios (0.5 to 2.0) on the X-axis.

Completeness of facility maternal death reporting by community-to-institutional ratio

Interpretation guidelines

Not all modeled scenarios apply equally to every country context. Teams should evaluate and narrow down the outputs based on local evidence:

- If external validation indicates that the true national population MMR sits below the UN median baseline, pick the scenario corresponding to the lowest population MMR boundary (the lower-bound line).
- If contextual country data indicates that community maternal mortality is roughly 1.5 to 2.0 times higher than facility mortality, the corresponding reporting completeness range is narrowed to 62%–69%.

By default, DataSuite processes calculations using community-to-institutional ratios of 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 to establish baseline tracking boundaries.

A similar approach can be used for stillbirths using all births instead of live births.
The UN global stillbirth estimates for 2021 with uncertainty ranges can be used (lower and upper bound are 90% uncertainty intervals from the model). There is little research on the community to institutional stillbirth ratio (partly because community level stillbirth reporting is more uncertain) but it is likely that the ratios are lower than for maternal mortality, as institutional mortality levels are much higher for stillbirth rates than for MMR. A range of 0.5-2.0 may be used for the estimation of the level of completeness of facility reporting.

Completeness of facility stillbirth reporting by community-to-institutional ratio

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
- Treating institutional mortality as population mortality. Facilities capture only part of deaths.
- Comparing regions with very different shares of institutional births.
- Ignoring completeness. A low completeness means the reported rate is a lower bound.

sections.heading: In the apps
sections.text: The Mortality group is in the RMNCAH app only; Mortality has the screen-by-screen guide.

sections.heading: Institutional Mortality
sections.text: Under Mortality in the Analysis group. The first card shows the rates (Maternal Mortality, Still Birth Rate, Neonatal Deaths), with regions as dots and the country as a line, by year. The second card, Institutional Mortality DQA, shows fresh stillbirths as a percentage of all stillbirths, the stillbirth to maternal death ratio, and neonatal deaths per maternal death.

sections.heading: Mortality Mapping
sections.text: Maps Maternal Mortality and Still Birth Rate by region for the selected years.

sections.heading: Mortality Completeness
sections.text: The Institutional MMR and Institutional SBR tabs show the completeness of facility reporting for the lower bound, median and upper bound of the UN estimate, across community-to-institutional ratios.

pages.title: Curative health services utilization for sick children

sections.heading: Curative health services utilization for sick children
sections.text:
Routine health facility data on outpatient visits and hospital admissions show how far children under 5 reach curative services, and facility case fatality serves as a proxy for the quality of clinical care. This step produces these indicators at national and sub-national level.

At a glance

- Answers: How much outpatient and inpatient care do children under 5 receive, and what does facility case fatality suggest about the quality of clinical care?
- Uses: OPD visits (new visits and re-visits) and hospital admissions (new admissions and re-admissions), for children under 5 and individuals 5 years and older, adjusted for incomplete reporting and extreme outliers in data adjustment (case fatality uses unadjusted data); the DHIS2 projected under-5 population.
- Produces: OPD visits per child per year, the under-5 share of OPD visits, admissions per 100 children under 5 per year, the under-5 share of admissions and the pediatric case fatality rate, nationally and by region; the utilization rates are compared with health system inputs in health system performance.
- In the apps: Service utilization and health system (RMNCAH app only).

sections.heading: Scientific basis for the analysis
sections.text:
There is limited routine information regarding curative service utilization, even though diarrhea and pneumonia remain leading causes of child mortality. Service utilization statistics on care-seeking behavior among children with recent illnesses (diarrhea, acute respiratory infection, or fever in the preceding 2 weeks) are traditionally obtained from household surveys, which rely on maternal recall.

Routine health facility data on outpatient department (OPD) visits serves as a direct indicator of access to curative services: fewer than one visit per person per year is generally considered an indicator of poor geographic or financial access. Similarly, data on hospital admissions reflects service access, while institutional facility-based mortality (case fatality) serves as a proxy indicator for the quality of clinical care.

sections.heading: Description of analytical steps
sections.text:
The data on OPD visits must include both new visits and re-visits. These data are usually stratified into two main cohorts: children under 5 years of age, and individuals 5 years and older.

As with maternal care, newborn care, and immunization metrics, data quality is systematically assessed first. Adjustments are applied to correct for incomplete reporting, and extreme outliers are resolved. This adjusted, clean dataset is then utilized for trends and comparative analyses at both national and sub-national tiers.

sections.heading: Outpatient service utilization
sections.text: Outpatient department data inputs must include both new visits and re-visits combined.

sections.heading: Mean number of OPD visits per child per year
sections.text:
To track the frequency of care-seeking coverage, the metric is structured as follows:

- Numerator: Adjusted number of under-5 OPD visits within a calendar year.
- Denominator: Total projected population of children under 5 years of age extracted from the DHIS2 projections.

Mathematically, this rate is expected to remain highly stable over time, with an expected variance of less than 0.2 visits per child per year between consecutive reporting periods. A gradual, steady increase over time points to either genuine improvements in physical access to OPD services or an escalating disease burden within the pediatric population.

While there is no rigid global cut-off threshold, an attendance rate of fewer than 1 visit per year per child indicates that access barriers are likely restricting service utilization. OPD statistics are routinely calculated and tracked at the national and regional/provincial levels.

sections.heading: Percent of OPD visits contributed by children under five years
sections.text:
This metric serves as an internal check for data consistency. The proportion of under-5 visits typically accounts for 15% to 45% of all recorded outpatient consultations.

- In high-fertility settings (e.g., countries with a Total Fertility Rate > 4), this proportion is expected to sit on the higher end of the spectrum, frequently exceeding 30%.
- Data quality flags: If the calculated percentage falls completely outside the 15%–45% boundary, a data quality issue may be present. Furthermore, a sudden shift between years exceeding 5 percentage points flags potential reporting inconsistency.

sections.heading: Inpatient service utilization
sections.text:
The data on hospital admissions include both new admissions and re-admissions. These records are stratified by age into under-5 and 5 years and over cohorts. Where available, patient discharge data (calculated as: $\text{Discharges} = \text{Admissions} - \text{Deaths}$) is the preferred analytical input.

A review of reporting completeness and the presence of extreme outliers is used to evaluate inpatient data quality. Because reporting rates from hospitals and facilities with inpatient departments (IPD) can be more complex to track than routine outpatient data, the decision to adjust for incomplete reporting relies heavily on the technical judgment of the country team regarding registry reliability.

Extreme monthly outliers are common in inpatient data due to compilation errors; corrective adjustments must be applied cautiously. It is highly recommended to assess and compare both the unadjusted and adjusted data outputs side-by-side.

sections.heading: Number of admissions per 100 children under 5 per year
sections.text:
This serves as a core indicator of inpatient access capacity. A calculated value of fewer than 2 admissions per 100 children under-5 per year indicates very low access to acute inpatient services. For context, the median baseline across sub-Saharan African countries for the 2018–2022 period was 4.5 admissions per year.

Annual fluctuations are expected to be minimal; a year-to-year shift of 1 or more admissions per 100 children is highly unlikely under normal circumstances unless tied to a documented emergency, such as an epidemic or outbreak.

sections.heading: Percent of admissions contributed by children under five years
sections.text:
This is used as a data quality validation indicator. The percentage typically ranges between 10% and 40% of all recorded facility admissions.

If the value falls outside this specific reference interval, it points to either an underlying data quality issue or an exceptional epidemiological event. A year-to-year fluctuation exceeding 5 percentage points flags an active data quality problem.

sections.heading: Case fatality rate
sections.text:
The case fatality rate serves as a key proxy indicator for the quality of clinical care within facility wards. It is mathematically defined as:

$\text{Pediatric Case Fatality Rate} = \frac{\text{Number of Children Who Die in Hospital}}{\text{Total Number of Admissions (Discharges + Deaths)}}$

Methodological rule: Case fatality calculations must be performed using unadjusted data inputs exclusively. The platform does not apply reporting completeness adjustments or outlier corrections to either the raw number of institutional deaths or total admissions in this module.

A lower case fatality rate within health facilities corresponds directly to a higher standard of acute clinical care.

sections.heading: MCH preventive vs curative index
sections.text:
The index places each Admin 1 region by its use of preventive and of curative services for children under 5:

- MCH Preventive services index: antenatal, delivery, postnatal and immunization services per child under 5, weighted by importance.
- Curative service use index: OPD visits and IPD admissions per child under 5, with admissions counted ten times a visit.

Median lines divide the regions into four quadrants: low or high preventive, and low or high curative.

sections.text:
OPD visits per person per year, all ages and under 5

Map of under-5 OPD visits per child per year by region

Sub-national distribution of under-5 OPD visits per capita by region

OPD interpretation considerations:

When compiling the interpretation narrative for the OPD sub-module, answer the following evaluation questions directly:

- Data quality baseline: What can be concluded about the data quality for OPD visits? Is there a high level of consistency in the reported raw numbers between consecutive years?
- Temporal trends: What is the exact calculated number of OPD visits per child per year across the 2019–2023 timeline, and is it demonstrating an upward trend?
- Access barriers: Is the national or sub-national rate lower than 1 visit per year, confirming low access to services?
- Geographical disparities: What do the data reveal about OPD visits per child per year across different regions or provinces in 2023? How large is the absolute margin between the top-performing and bottom-performing sub-national units?

Percentage of under-5 OPD visits and IPD admissions by year

sections.heading: Inpatient admissions and case fatality
sections.text:
IPD admissions per 100 persons by year, all ages and under 5

IPD interpretation considerations:

Your narrative analysis for the inpatient sub-module must explicitly evaluate the following parameters:

- Data consistency: Is there internal consistency in the reported raw numbers of admissions and overall admission rates over time?
- Access metrics: What is the absolute number of admissions per 100 children under 5 per year across the 2019–2023 trend lines?
- Sub-national spread: Is the observed rate high or low compared to historical benchmarks? What specific sub-national patterns emerge when evaluating admissions per 100 children under 5 across regions or provinces?

Case fatality rate (%) by year

sections.heading: Subnational analysis
sections.text:
Subnational analysis asks how coverage varies between regions (Admin1) and districts (Admin2), whether geographic inequality is reducing, and how many units reach coverage targets. It produces subnational coverage estimates, the regional one-pager, the MADM inequality measure and the percentage of units meeting each target.

At a glance

- Answers: How does coverage vary across regions and districts? Have inequalities between subnational units reduced? What percentage of regions and districts meet each target?
- Uses: the same adjustment (Data adjustment) and the best-performing denominator (Denominator selection) as the national analysis (National coverage).
- Produces: coverage by region and district, the regional subnational statistical summary (one-pager) with the composite coverage index, the MADM, and the percentage of units meeting each target; used in the reports (Reports).
- In the apps: Sub-national analysis; national inequality and targets in Coverage, equity and targets.
- Defaults: Subnational

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text:
Subnational analysis reveals the geographic distribution of health service access—critical for identifying underperforming districts that drag down national averages and for targeting resources where they are most needed. This module estimates coverage at regional (Admin1) and district (Admin2) levels using the same denominator and adjustment methodology as national analysis, then visualizes how coverage varies across geography. Expect more volatility at district level due to small populations, referral patterns, and facility location choices (hospitals in towns serve surrounding rural areas), but this noise contains actionable intelligence about where health systems fail.

DataSuite generates district-level "one-pagers"—visual summaries pairing facility-based trend lines (2020–2024) alongside recent survey snapshots, comparison bar graphs showing each district's performance relative to peers, and composite coverage indices averaging seven mother-and-child-health indicators. These one-pagers communicate coverage reality to decision-makers in accessible, locally-contextualized formats, making it impossible to ignore geographic inequities and facilitating evidence-based allocation of health system strengthening investments.

sections.heading: Subnational coverage
sections.text:
Subnational analysis of health intervention coverage is essential for advancing universal health coverage (UHC), which aims to ensure equitable access to quality health services for all populations. National averages often mask critical disparities that exist across regions, districts, or population subgroups.

National averages hide the regions and districts that are being left behind, and regions and districts are where programme action is usually targeted. Monitoring subnational data helps identify geographical areas where coverage is low, signaling potential inequities in health service access and prompting targeted interventions. This is particularly important for drawing attention to populations who are left behind and ensuring resources are directed where they are most needed.

sections.heading: Inequality and global coverage targets
sections.text: Reducing geographic inequality is essential for equitable health systems and achieving the SDGs. Subnational inequalities reveal inconsistencies in service delivery and highlight systemic barriers to healthcare access. Tracking inequality indicators helps assess whether health systems are becoming more equitable and whether targeted interventions are working.

sections.heading: Coverage estimates at Admin1 and Admin2
sections.text:
The focus here is to assess the coverage estimates (e.g., ANC4, institutional deliveries, Penta3) at Admin1 and Admin2 levels using the best performing denominator for the coverage computations, as decided from the analysis in section 2 on denominators.

There will be more "noise" in the subnational data with improbably high or low coverage rates, compared to the national analyses, and more so in the district analyses than in the regional (Admin1) analyses. This is because district analyses are affected by small numbers (more fluctuations which may be random or due to data quality issues) and by the health service utilization patterns by women and children. For instance, a municipal district may get more deliveries than an adjacent rural district because of the location of the hospitals in the municipal district. Small numbers, patient movement between districts and reporting gaps all produce implausibly high or low values.

sections.heading: Subnational statistical summaries (one-pager)
sections.text:
The aim is to produce a one-pager for each Admin1 unit (generally region, province or county) that contains the regional information as well as a summary of the districts within the region. We refer to this as the regional subnational statistical summary.

The following components are included:

- Summary of key demographic information for the region and the districts: A table with the expected number of births in 2024 according to the DHIS2 projections and according to the preferred denominators derived from the health facility data (based on ANC1 for live births, and on penta1 for immunization indicators).
- Line graphs with the trend in coverage of institutional deliveries and penta3 vaccination: These include the best estimates for 2020–2024 based on the health facility data, as well as the estimates from the most recent surveys (from 2015) for the same indicators (with confidence intervals if possible).
- Bar graphs that compare the 2024 coverage situation in the region compared to all other regions: This puts the region into the lowest, middle, or upper third of regions in terms of coverage. This is done for both institutional deliveries and penta3 vaccination.
- Table that summarizes the coverage for institutional deliveries and penta3 vaccination in 2024 by district: A localized breakdown of performance across the subnational area.

Other indicators can be used as prioritized by the country (e.g., ANC4, measles1).

Template layout of the regional subnational statistical summary one-pager:

Template of the regional subnational statistical summary one-pager

To summarize the coverage situation according to the health facility statistics for 2024 can be done for the regional level and shown on a map. A composite coverage index is computed as an average in seven mother and child health indicators: ANC4, institutional live birth coverage, SBA, IPT2, postnatal care, pentavalent vaccine 3rd dosage and measles 1 vaccination coverage. Equal weight is given to all indicators.

sections.heading: MADM and units above a target
sections.text:
Here we calculate the Median Absolute Deviation from the Median (MADM) to quantify the spread in coverage among districts within an Admin1 level, compared with the coverage at that specific Admin1 subnational unit.

The key statistical measures for subnational inequalities are:

- MADM (Median Absolute Deviation from the Median): This measure gives an indication of whether the country has been successful in reducing inequalities between subnational units.
- Percent of subnational units with coverage above a specific target or threshold: This indicator provides information on the extent to which a country has been successful in reaching universal coverage at the subnational level.

sections.heading: Progress towards targets
sections.text:
Summary of district and regional performance:

Progress towards international and national targets can be measured by computing the percentage of regions and districts that have achieved these targets. The goal is for all regions and districts to have met the target. Higher percentages mean less (geographic) inequality.

sections.heading: Target values
sections.text:
The 2024 Countdown vaccination guidebook uses these targets:

Indicator | Target | Source
Institutional delivery | 80% of districts with coverage of at least 80% | EPMM / ENAP
Routine immunization | 90% coverage for all routine vaccines | IA2030
DTP3 (Penta-3) | Geographic equity: coverage in the 20% of districts with the lowest coverage | IA2030
DTP3 (Penta-3) | At least 80% in every district |

The apps count a unit as meeting the target when:

Indicator | Unit meets the target when
BCG, Penta-3, Measles-1 | Coverage is at least 90% (national) or at least 80% (region or district)
ANC-4 | Coverage is at least 70%
Institutional live births | Coverage is at least 80%
Dropout Penta-1 to Penta-3, Penta-3 to Measles-1 | Dropout is below 10%

The apps report the percentage of units meeting each target. A target such as "Penta-3 at least 80% in every district" is met when that percentage reaches 100%. The geographic equity measure (Penta-3 coverage in the 20% of districts with the lowest coverage) is not computed by the apps.

RMNCAH and vaccine analyses differ here: the ANC-4 and institutional live births targets apply to RMNCAH analyses and the dropout targets to vaccine analyses; the vaccine targets apply to both. The Coverage Target page has the tabs ANC 4 Visits, Institutional Live Births and Vaccine in the RMNCAH app, and Vaccine and Dropout in the Vaxx app. See RMNCAH and vaccine analyses.

sections.heading: Subnational coverage
sections.text:
Check a map's legend before you use it. The guidebook: if the legend shows only a few percentage points between the gradings, small differences look large; do not use the map.

- Compare the region with the national line. A survey point far from the DHIS2 line in one region often signals a denominator or reporting problem there. Check the reporting rate of the region (Data quality) before drawing conclusions.

District denominators are the least reliable. A district with coverage over 100 percent, or one that flips between years, is more likely to have a population or reporting problem than a real change. Cross-check it against the district's data quality.

sections.heading: Inequality
sections.text:
In the inequality charts each dot is a subnational unit and the line is the national (or regional) coverage.

- A wide spread of dots means high inequality: the national average hides weak areas.
- A spread that narrows over the years means inequality is falling. The MADM summarises this spread.
- A district that is always low is different from one that is low only in a bad year: the second case may be a data problem.
- Facility inequality between regions can come from denominator or reporting differences, not real differences in access.

sections.heading: Global coverage targets
sections.text:
- A rising percentage of units meeting the target is good news only if coverage does not exceed plausible levels. Check units far above 100 percent for denominator problems.
- For dropout, remember that lower is better.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
- Reading a single district year in isolation. Look at the trend and the neighbouring years.
- Small districts give noisy percentages. Read several years, not one.
- Comparing regions that have very different populations without checking numerators.
- Comparing Admin 1 and Admin 2 results directly: units differ in size and reliability.
- Forgetting that the denominator selected for the whole country also drives regional results. If one region looks impossible (above 100%), test another denominator before flagging the region.
- Ranking areas on the latest year only. Combine level, change over time, reporting completeness and denominator quality, as in National coverage > Best and worst subnational performance.

sections.heading: In the apps
sections.text: The Sub-National Analysis group has three pages; Sub-national analysis has the screen-by-screen guide. National inequality and national targets are in Coverage, equity and targets. In the Vaxx app the indicator tabs and Custom Check cover the vaccination indicators.

sections.heading: Sub-National Coverage
sections.text:
Navigate to the Sub-National Analysis tab -> Sub-National Coverage and select the admin level of interest (Region (Admin Level1) or District). Then select the indicator of interest from the key indicators (ANC4, Institutional deliveries, Low Birth Weight, Penta 1 and Measles 1). You can also use the Custom Check tab to select any other indicator of interest.

Subnational coverage tab showing institutional live births coverage estimates over time

sections.heading: Sub-National Inequality
sections.text:
Navigate to the Sub-National Analysis tab -> Sub-National Inequality and inspect the plotted regional and district results by year, with the median absolute deviation from the median (MADM), as the summary measure to assess if inequalities have reduced.

Subnational inequality tab showing the MADM by year for institutional live births

sections.heading: Coverage Target
sections.text:
Navigate to the Sub-National Analysis tab -> Coverage Target and read the percentage of districts in a region meeting each target, by year. The table lists the districts meeting the target for the indicator and year you select.

Coverage target tab showing the percentage of subnational units meeting the vaccine target

sections.heading: Data dictionary
sections.text:
The apps' data names things with short ids -- an indicator (penta1), a denominator option (anc1derived), a target population (totinftpenta) -- combined into column names such as cov_penta3_penta1derived. This page says what each part means. Read the meaning here rather than from the spelling: anc1 and penta1 are the ANC1-derived and Penta1-derived denominators, while anc1derived and penta1derived are the population-growth options.

Generated from cd2030.core 1.3.0. In R, cd2030.core::cd_dictionary() returns these tables and cd2030.core::cd_describe_columns() reads column names with them.

sections.heading: Denominators
sections.text:
The six denominator options (Denominator assessment and selection).

Id | Label | What it is | Levels

anc1 | ANC1-derived | Derived each year from that year's reported ANC1 visits and the survey's ANC1 coverage: pregnancies = ANC1 / ANC1 survey coverage, then deliveries, births and infants from them. | national, adminlevel_1, district

sections.heading: Defaults and thresholds
sections.text:
The numbers the method uses -- default values, cut-offs and expected ranges -- in one place, grouped by analysis step. Each row says what the number is, whether it applies to RMNCAH analyses, vaccine analyses or both, how the apps use it, and which section of the Countdown methodology explains it.

The values are generated from the apps' code (cd2030.core), so they are what the apps use. Where the 2024 Countdown vaccination guidebook differs, the methodology page says so.

sections.heading: Data quality
sections.text:
The checks of reporting completeness, outliers and internal consistency, and the overall quality score: Data quality assessment.
District reporting completeness threshold (1b): 90 % (both). Score item 1b is the percentage of districts whose facility reporting rate is at least this value; the app starts at 90% and the Reporting Rate page can change it.
Reporting threshold quick picks: 70, 80, 90, 95 % (both). The values the Reporting Rate page offers as quick picks for the district reporting threshold.
Extreme outlier bound: 5 x MAD (both). A monthly value is an extreme outlier when it lies more than 5 median absolute deviations from its district's median (Hampel X84).
Outlier baseline years: all years except the latest (both). The district median and MAD used for the outlier bounds are computed from all years except the latest, so the latest year cannot hide its own outliers.
Adequate range for consistency ratios: 1-1.5 ratio (both). A district's consistency ratio (the ratio of its annual totals) is adequate when it is between 1 and 1.5 inclusive.
Consistency ratios checked: anc1/penta1, penta1/penta3 (both). The internal consistency ratios checked for every indicator group (numerator/denominator).
Consistency ratios added for immunization: opv1/opv3 (vaccine). The consistency ratios added to the common ones when the indicator group is vaccine.
ANC1/Penta1 expected ratio multiplier: 1.07 ratio (both). The expected anc1/penta1 ratio is multiplied by this factor to allow for mortality between the first antenatal visit and the first Penta dose.
Assumed anc1 coverage for expected ratios: 0.98 proportion (both). When no survey coverage is supplied, calculate_ratios_summary() builds the expected ratios from an assumed anc1 coverage of 98% (the app passes the country's survey estimates instead).
Assumed penta1 coverage for expected ratios: 0.97 proportion (both). When no survey coverage is supplied, calculate_ratios_summary() builds the expected ratios from an assumed penta1 coverage of 97% (the app passes the country's survey estimates instead).
Assumed penta3 coverage for expected ratios: 0.89 proportion (both). When no survey coverage is supplied, calculate_ratios_summary() builds the expected ratios from an assumed penta3 coverage of 89% (the app passes the country's survey estimates instead).
Assumed opv1 coverage for expected ratios: 0.97 proportion (vaccine). When no survey coverage is supplied, calculate_ratios_summary() builds the expected ratios from an assumed opv1 coverage of 97% (the app passes the country's survey estimates instead).
Assumed opv3 coverage for expected ratios: 0.78 proportion (vaccine). When no survey coverage is supplied, calculate_ratios_summary() builds the expected ratios from an assumed opv3 coverage of 78% (the app passes the country's survey estimates instead).
Assumed pcv1 coverage for expected ratios: 0.97 proportion (vaccine). When no survey coverage is supplied, calculate_ratios_summary() builds the expected ratios from an assumed pcv1 coverage of 97% (the app passes the country's survey estimates instead).
Assumed rota1 coverage for expected ratios: 0.96 proportion (vaccine). When no survey coverage is supplied, calculate_ratios_summary() builds the expected ratios from an assumed rota1 coverage of 96% (the app passes the country's survey estimates instead).
Overall score components (RMNCAH): 1a, 1b, 1c, 2a, 2b, 3c, 3d (rmncah). The annual data quality score is the mean of these rows of the overall score table: reporting, completeness, outliers and the share of districts with adequate ratios.
Overall score components (immunization): 1a, 1b, 1c, 2a, 2b, 3f, 3g, 3h (vaccine). The annual data quality score is the mean of these rows of the overall score table: reporting, completeness, outliers and the share of districts with adequate ratios.

sections.heading: Data adjustment
sections.text:
The adjustment for incomplete reporting (the factor $k$), low reporting rates and extreme outliers: Data adjustment.
Completeness adjustment factor k (default adjustment): 0.25 (both). adjust_service_data(adjustment = "default") uses k = 0.25 for every indicator group (anc, idelv, pnc, vacc, opd, ipd).
Starting k in the app: 0 (both). A new dataset starts with k = 0 for every indicator group, so the app adjusts nothing until the user picks a k on the Data Adjustment page.
k values offered: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1 (both). The k values the Data Adjustment page offers for each indicator group.
Reporting rate cutoff: 75 % (both). Before adjusting, a reporting rate below 75% (or missing) is replaced by the district's median reporting rate.
Reporting rates used for the replacement median: 75-100 % (both). The replacement median is taken over the district's reporting rates between 75% and 100% inclusive.
Outliers replaced after adjustment: 5 x MAD (both). After the k adjustment, values more than 5 MAD from the district's median monthly value (baseline: all years except the latest) are replaced by the median of the district's other (non-outlier) months in the same year; missing months get the district's median for that year.

sections.heading: Denominators
sections.text:
The assumptions behind the derived denominators and the checks of the population projections: Denominator assessment and selection.
Neonatal mortality rate: 0.025 proportion (both). Default neonatal mortality rate (2.5%) of calculate_indicator_coverage() when no rate is supplied; the rate it is given also fills in regions the survey has no value for.
Post-neonatal mortality rate: 0.024 proportion (both). Default post-neonatal mortality rate (2.4%) of calculate_indicator_coverage() when no rate is supplied; the rate it is given also fills in regions the survey has no value for.
Stillbirth rate: 0.02 proportion (both). Default stillbirth rate (2%) of calculate_indicator_coverage() when no rate is supplied; the rate it is given also fills in regions the survey has no value for.
Twin rate: 0.015 proportion (both). Default twin rate (1.5%) of calculate_indicator_coverage() when no rate is supplied; the rate it is given also fills in regions the survey has no value for.
Pregnancy loss rate: 0.03 proportion (both). Default pregnancy loss rate (3%) of calculate_indicator_coverage() when no rate is supplied; the rate it is given also fills in regions the survey has no value for.
ANC1 survey coverage: 0.98 proportion (both). Default ANC1 survey coverage (98%) of calculate_indicator_coverage() when no rate is supplied; the rate it is given also fills in regions the survey has no value for.
Penta1 (DTP1) survey coverage: 0.97 proportion (both). Default Penta1 (DTP1) survey coverage (97%) of calculate_indicator_coverage() when no rate is supplied; the rate it is given also fills in regions the survey has no value for.
Survey year: 2019 year (both). Default survey year in calculate_indicator_coverage(); the app uses the year of the country's latest survey.
Starting twin and pregnancy loss rates in the app: 0.015-0.03 proportion (both). A new dataset starts with a twin rate of 1.5% and a pregnancy loss rate of 3%; neonatal, post-neonatal and stillbirth rates come from the survey.

sections.heading: Coverage
sections.text:
National coverage and its comparison with surveys and targets: National coverage.
Vaccine coverage target (national): 90 % (both). At national level a vaccine (BCG, Penta3, measles1) reaches the target when its coverage is at least this value.
ANC4 coverage target: 70 % (rmncah). Units reach the ANC4 target when their coverage is at least this value.
Institutional live births coverage target: 80 % (rmncah). Units reach the institutional live births target when their coverage is at least this value.
Dropout rate target: 10 % (vaccine). Units meet the dropout target (Penta1-Penta3, Penta3-measles1) when their dropout rate is below this value.
High performer threshold (other indicators): 80 % (both). CacheConnection$get_high_performers() lists the units at or above this coverage for indicators without a specific target.

sections.heading: Subnational
sections.text:
Subnational coverage, inequality and the coverage targets: Subnational analysis.
Vaccine coverage target (regions and districts): 80 % (both). Below national level a vaccine (BCG, Penta3, measles1) reaches the target when its coverage is at least this value.

sections.heading: Mortality
sections.text:
Institutional mortality, its plausibility checks and the completeness of death reporting: Mortality.
Very low institutional MMR: 25 per 100,000 live births (rmncah). A unit whose institutional maternal mortality ratio is below this value is flagged as very low, a sign of under-reported deaths.
Very low institutional stillbirth rate: 6 per 1,000 births (rmncah). A unit whose institutional stillbirth rate is below this value is flagged as very low, a sign of under-reported stillbirths.
Completeness ratios compared: 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 ratio (rmncah). The completeness ratios at which the institutional mortality is compared with the UN estimates.
